speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the mining exploration industry in Canada can play an important role in the economic recovery, especially in the resource regions of Canada. I ask the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Department of Finance in Ottawa to take seriously the demands made by the Quebec prospectors association in December 1992.

Mr. Speaker, today is Aboriginal Languages Day, a proud occasion to celebrate the survival and richness of the 53 aboriginal languages spoken in Canada.
I am proud to say that the Northwest Territories has six official aboriginal languages: Chipewyan, Cree, Dogrib, Gwich'in, Inuktitut and Slavey. All six languages have equal status, rights and privileges with English and French within the NWT, including use in government services and communications.
Statistics show that 50 of Canada's 53 aboriginal languages are declining, endangered or facing extinction. In this year of indigenous peoples this government should provide the funding needed to promote language awareness and the revival of aboriginal languages in communities which are most threatened.
[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Slavey, translated as follows:]

The Dene language is a gift from the Creator and we must work to preserve it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through a number of legislative initiatives which all opposition parties have attempted to derail, the government has restrained public spending in five major areas.
It has done so by reducing the rate of growth of transfers to provinces, for instance Bill C-32 and Bill C-60; by streamlining the operations of government, for instance Bill C-20, Bill C-21, BUI C-56, BUI C-63, BUI C-69 and BUI C-93; through the privatization of Crown corporations, for instance BUI C-8, Bill C-13, and BUI C-38; by restraining the salaries of public officials, for instance, BUI C-26, Bill C-55, BUI C-76 and BUI C-113; and by restraining grants and contributions to organizations.
The result of our ongoing efforts is that since 1987 we have run the operations of government in the black.

Mr. Speaker, using the most recent figures avaUable, the Roeher Institute estimates disabUities cost Canada and Canadians some $19.5 bUlion a year. That is a lot of money and the bUl goes up each year.
For this reason alone all levels of government, as well as business and labour, should be finding ways to co-operate in order to deal with and address these costs and the effects of disabUity in our society.

March 31, 1993
However we must never forget that disabilities affect Canadians where they live: in their families and in their communities. The Canadian Association of Community Living is working to ensure that mentally handicapped people can live at home, go to the local school and take a job. Allowing people with disabilities to take their rightful place as full members of our society ought to be our goal.
Independence and integration of persons with disabilities makes not only good economic sense but it respects the rights of citizens and promotes social and political values that will benefit us all.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all Canadians and all my colleagues in the House and in my own name, I wish to pay tribute to a great Canadian who died last night at the age of 61.
Mr. Mouton's contribution to the sporting and social life of Quebecers can never be forgotten. Last Saturday night, he was still behind the microphone in the Forum. When I saw him there I remarked to my wife how courageous he was.

It is with great admiration for him and for what he did that in the name of each and every one of us I thank him.

I speak for everyone in the House in offering his wife and children our deepest sympathy.

subtopic: THE PREMIER OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
THE PREMIER OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate a former colleague in this House, Catherine Callbeck, who on Monday made history by becoming the first woman elected premier in Canada.
Under Premier Callbeck's leadership the Liberal team won 55 per cent of the popular vote in the election and won a landslide victory with 31 seats in the legislature. In
a campaign based on positive ideas and a concern for the future the Liberal Party distinguished itself.
I wish to congratulate the many fine members of the Prince Edward Island legislature. After seven years of fine Liberal government Islanders can look forward to four more years of a strong Liberal administration.
The mandate from the people is clear, and I know that Premier Callbeck is up to the task.

Mr. Speaker, two days ago we in the Reform Party of Canada released our plan to eliminate the federal deficit in three years and save Canada's social programs from complete collapse.
This plan has met with favourable editorials across the country. Our zero in three plan is based on: first, fairness, that federal spending reductions should be distributed fairly across all major areas of federal expenditure; second, the principle of leadership by example; and, third, the principle of priorizing social spending.
The debt has increased under Tory mismanagement from $180 billion in 1984 to $460 billion today. Thirty-two cents out of every tax dollar is being spent on interest, leaving only 68 cents for funding government programs and services.
Yet the government says its hands are tied, that there is nothing it can do about it, and deficit reduction requires constitutional amendments. The fact of the matter is that neither the Progressive Conservatives, the Liberals, nor the New Democratic Party have any plan to reduce the deficit. In fact they plan to increase spending and increase the debt.
The Reform Party is the only party that can stop the haemorrhaging and save our social safety nets.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has just scored a coup. Canadians should take pride in Monday's announcement by the Financial Network Association that it had chosen Ottawa for its one-stop shopping financial data network.
March 31, 1993

The expertise of Canadian telecommunications is world renowned, and for this reason Canada is quickly becoming the nerve centre for financial information.
Telecommunications is one of the engines of growth in the Canadian economy, and the implications of this announcement are enormous. We have just been elevated to the forefront of this $30 billion a year industry.
This is good news for all Canadians and speaks well of our country's good standing within the international community.

subtopic: THE LATE CLAUDE MOUTON AND DANNY GALLIVAN
THE LATE CLAUDE MOUTON AND DANNY GALLIVAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night, the Canadiens hockey team lost another of its spokesmen. Claude Mouton, the well-known announcer who worked in the Montreal Forum for the Canadiens, died at the age of 61. How can we forget Claude Mouton, in his well-known style, welcoming the Canadiens onto the ice?
Indeed, for over 21 years, Claude's voice stirred the Forum crowds.

Recently another legend at the Forum, hockey broadcaster Danny Gallivan, passed away. Together these two men were institutions in Montreal, and their association with sport and particularly the Montreal Canadiens was enjoyed by hockey fans across Canada.
It is only when people like Claude Mouton and Danny Gallivan leave us that we realize how much they meant to the game of hockey and to those of us who grew up listening to them.
As a former NHL official, I have fond memories of these gentlemen. I will always remember their contribution to hockey, their love for the game, the pride they took in their work and, most important, the enjoyment they provided to the fans.

Mr. Speaker, again I am urging the Department of Agriculture to accept the formula outlined by the Atlantic Farmers Council when the 10 per cent reduction is applied to the Feed Freight Assistance Program.
The current proposed formula contradicts the Feed Freight Assistance Act by abandoning the primary principle of the act, which is to ensure fair equalization of feed grain prices throughout Canada.
The impact on Atlantic Canada is 50 times as much as it is on Ontario under the present proposed plan. Also any change in the Atlantic subsidy should not take place until the same reduction takes place in the west.
The provinces do not agree with the present plan; the industry is against it; and it contradicts the principle of the act. I respectfully request that this plan not be implemented, and that it be replaced by one that is fair to all farmers.

Tansi. Mr. Speaker, today, March 31, is Aboriginal Languages Day.
In March 1989 Canada's chiefs attending a special meeting of the Assembly of First Nations unanimously passed a resolution declaring March 31 of each year Aboriginal Languages Day.
The chiefs did so to promote and enhance an awareness and revival of aboriginal languages and to celebrate the survival and richness of the 53 aboriginal languages spoken in Canada.
The Assembly of First Nations is calling for the recognition of aboriginal languages in Canada during 1993, the International Year for World Indigenous Peoples.
It is time for Parliament to accept the AFN proposal and recognize the unique contribution these languages have made to Canada, as well as the essential role language plays in the maintenance and development of culture and well-being among First Nations people. Tenake.

March 31, 1993
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, thank you for your simply outstanding presentation this morning at the national prayer breakfast. Kinanaskomtin Daytapewkimaw.
In 1989, recognizing the need for a day to draw attention to the fact that aboriginal languages were at risk, the chiefs of First Nations in assembly declared March 31 Aboriginal Languages Day.
As our colleague, the member for Western Arctic, said today is a day when First Nations celebrate the survival and richness of the 53 aboriginal languages spoken in Canada.
I ask this Elouse to recognize all aboriginal languages in this International Year for World Indigenous Peoples. I also call on all First Nations to continue their dedicated efforts to ensure the survival of our languages.
The manifestation of our spirit, mind and body, the development of our positive self-esteem and pride is through the use of our own languages.
[[DOT]Editor's note: Member spoke in Cree, translated as follows:]

Let us teach each other and use our languages the Great Spirit gave us.

Mr. Speaker, today the headlines are shouting what the Liberals have suspected all along, that Canadians are paying higher prices for drugs than most industrialized countries.
What a coincidence that this damning evidence was released after the government forced Bill C-91 through Parliament. What a coincidence that a public forum to look at this evidence was held five days after, and not before, Bill C-91 was given royal assent. What a coincidence.
I have a message for this government. Its mandate is to protect the people of Canada and our health care system. Drug companies work for profit, for the bottom line.
I urge the government to roll back drug prices, to start working for Canadians and for medicare, and not to let drug company bottom lines call the tune to which the government dances.

Mr. Speaker, I am in the process of filing a petition with 150,000 signatures requesting that this government deal with the issue of penalties for child molesters and child murderers.
These individuals believe that the people's voice to reinstate capital punishment should be heard. This government has avoided dealing with criminals who commit such heinous and immoral crimes.
Mrs. Barbara Wiebe of Calgary and her friends and colleagues have done an extraordinary job in co-ordinating and collecting signatures. I would like to take this opportunity to thank Mrs. Wiebe and all those involved in this massive effort.
In memory of Shannon Dawn Morrissette-Bird and all children who have suffered at the hands of others, I urge the government to introduce legislation to deal with these criminals.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 20, 1992, just a few days after the Westray coal mine blast claimed the lives of 26 men, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism stated: "What we will do of course is bring forward all the appropriate information as soon as possible". All the information. That is what the minister said then.
March 31, 1993

Yesterday senior legal counsel to the judicial inquiry in Nova Scotia was compelled to state publicly that this government, this minister, had declined to release the documents.
After almost one full year of stonewalling Parliament and hiding vital information from Canadians, will the minister now stand in his place, do the right thing and admit that he misled Parliament?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am going to stand in my place and make it very clear to this House that the hon. member has misled Parliament.
Yesterday the commission counsel made the following comment: "The inquiry does have an incomplete copy of the CANMET report which is obtained from a source other than the federal government". I stood in the House and said that this was not the case and that they in fact had received the CANMET report in its entirety.
I have just received a letter from the commission counsel. I will read it to the House: "I can confirm to you that the report identified by our file is the document which has been referred to as the CANMET report and that it was received from your client as part of the delivery of documents in June 1992".
I accept his apology and I hope to have the same from the hon. member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 9, 1992 when asked about the disclosure of the Westray mine documents the government House leader stated: "The government has been forthcoming with all of the background documents necessary for people to examine what has occurred and reach their own conclusions".
On December 1, 1992 the Prime Minister stated: "The position of this government will be to a full and complete co-operation with the public authorities in Nova Scotia".
Senior legal counsel yesterday said: "The inquiry does not have a copy of the memo to energy, mines and resources minister Jake Epp entitled 'Federal Funding of the Westray Coal Mine'".
Oral Questions
Will the minister stand in his place and tell the House that he has a second letter, that the inquiry has received that document and he is now going to disclose that to the Canadian public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we must remember. We must put this in perspective. We have to have a reality check here.
First of all the regulation of mines is a provincial responsibility. That is why there is a provincial commission of inquiry looking into it. Second, the federal government's role in this was only to give a loan guarantee. It is not to inspect the mine for safety but to give a loan guarantee which of course was our only participation.
What disturbs me is what the hon. member did yesterday. He brought documents in here. We are talking about the death of 26 miners. To get to the bottom of why they died is very important to everybody in Canada, including this House. The hon. member brought documents pertaining to this into this House. He has had them for three or four months and did not reveal it to the House until yesterday. If there is a cover-up, it is a cover-up by the hon. member.
The situation is this. We have co-operated with the commission and we are going to co-operate with the commission fully. We are going to co-operate fully because we want to get to the bottom of this matter. We want the Canadian people to know why these miners died. I think the hon. member should help us in that task.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what Canadians want from the minister responsible and all members of the cabinet are answers to the questions which have been plaguing Nova Scotians and particularly the families of the deceased miners.
The minister will know that 26 men have lost their lives. The inquiry has been suspended. Curragh has closed the mine. The taxpayers in Nova Scotia and in Ottawa have lost $12 million and $80 million respectively-
I ask that the minister make available to the public today the document with regard to the Westray funding

March 31, 1993
Oral Questions
and all of its contents to date so that Canadians will know that this government is trying to protect the political hides of the federal cabinet and the premier of Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am as willing as all members are every day to be partisan back and forth in this House. But when it comes to the death of 26 miners, the hon. member has gone far beyond what is appropriate.
He knows very well first of all that his facts are wrong and that $80 million has not yet been lost. The federal government holds title to the property that can be disposed of, certain funds of which could come back to the Crown.
More important, financial matters are not as important as these miners. What we want to do is get to the bottom of why they died. The commission of inquiry is going to do its work. It is going to be resuming its hearings in a matter of weeks. We will be tabling all of the relevant documents we said we would with them at that time.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the same minister and concerns the Westray Mine case. On May 9, 1992, 26 people lost their lives in the tragic explosion at the Westray Mine. Nearly $80 million in taxpayers' money has now been lost.
If what the minister says is true, is he prepared to table the missing pages in the House today? Is he prepared to do so, yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government has co-operated with the commission from the beginning and it will right to the end of its inquiries.
What I want to know from the hon. member is whether he and his party are going to apologize for raising an accusation yesterday in the House which was totally false, which has been confirmed by the commission counsel.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister just told us that he was prepared to co-operate with the inquiry commission. How does he explain the fact that yesterday, March 30, 1993, commission member John Merrick stated that the government had not released to the commission all the documents dealing with the Westray mine case.
Who is telling the truth, the minister or the Nova Scotia commission? Who is the minister trying to protect? Himself, his cabinet colleagues or the Premier of Nova Scotia who is in trouble?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the truth is that the commission lawyer had the courtesy and good grace to apologize for making a mistake. The hon. member does not seem to be willing to do that.
The hon. member has also asked for us to table further documents with the commission. We will do so as soon as it resumes its hearings.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
A major study today of seven industrialized countries has found that Canada's drug prices are among the highest in the world. They are 56 per cent higher than the international average. The evidence is clearly contrary to what Canadians were told during the debate on the drug patent legislation. Clearly something has gone very wrong.
Given the figures that have come out today, will the Deputy Prime Minister announce an inquiry into drug prices in Canada which will include why the prices are so high, the effects of the high prices on provincial and territorial budgets, and indeed the effect of the North American free trade deal on making it impossible to change this legislation if it is implemented?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have to be aware of what has happened with drug prices since 1987. Before BUI C-22 the increase in prices in Canada was 7.9 per cent per year. They have decreased to 2.6 per cent, which is
March 31, 1993

lower than the inflation rate. That is exactly what we said we would do in 1987 and it is exactly what we did. However at that time we did not have full control on the entry level prices with Bill C-22.
Bill C-91 had two specific purposes. One was to give protection in terms of intellectual property and development research and also to enforce the capacity of the PMPRB to control the price on entry and to control all prices.
We did exactly what we said we would do. The prices the member is referring to are prices which would be much higher if we had not done what we did in 1987 and 1991.
I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Sometimes I wonder if the whole government is inhaling.
Oh, oh.

The head of the government's own prices review board has said that these higher drug costs "are not consistent with the principle articulated in our mandate". Just last fall the government was told by Green Shield Inc. that the average cost of a claim for drugs after the government first protected the multinationals was more than double than before they did so. This change in legislation by this government is going to cost the provinces over $4 billion.
While this government is telling the provinces and territories to expect less and less health care and giving more and more profits to the multinational corporations, will the minister institute an inquiry into these unreasonably high drug prices?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly not comment on the premise that it is not the best question a member has asked since I have been in the House of Commons.
The hon. member is talking about an inquiry. She should first understand that the PMPRB is the board with the responsibility. It now works with the provinces to consider the prices of drugs and to act with regard to any price which is considered as unreasonable. That is what it did. That is what it will continue to do because its powers have been increased from what they were before.
Bill C-91 is a good bill. With regard to the question of the costs to the provinces, the hon. member should know
Oral Questions
because we have said time after time that patented drugs are 3 per cent of the volume of all drugs paid for by the provinces. If she would use the Conservative figures instead of the NDP figures maybe she would understand for once.

Mr. Speaker, the final fact is that it is not working. Canadian drug prices are too high and are higher than international drug prices. That is a fact.

With the North American Free Trade Agreement it will be impossible for the Government of Canada to change this legislation. In that case, people have the right to expect this government to backtrack. Otherwise it will be too late.
Will the government order an investigation to determine the long-term impact on the price of drugs and on health care budgets across the country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I said in English applies in French as well. We have no intention of conducting an investigation into the price of drugs, since we have the appropriate mechanisms to ensure that prices remain at reasonable levels for Canadian users.
As for health care costs, all provinces, including those with an NDP government, consider that the amounts invested in their health care systems are adequate. In fact, today, Quebec, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland have cut the amounts allocated to health care, because the amounts invested are sufficient. I repeat, we are not considering an investigation into the cost of drugs.

Mr. Speaker, I want to return to the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism.
On June 8, 1992, recognized in Hansard, page 11571, the minister at that time stated that all the information necessary was tabled in the House.

Maxell 31, 1993
Oral Questions
Today we have the minister admitting that the key document outlining the federal role in the funding of the Westray mine has not been made public. It has been withheld.
I want to ask the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism why this key document has not been made public and withheld. Why has the government stonewalled on this key issue outlining the federal responsibility and role in the Westray mine disaster? Why has it stonewalled for 10 months? Who is the minister trying to protect?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the hon. member and his colleagues have been playing politics with this issue through the whole of Question Period.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
He knows very well that we have already tabled 7,000 pages with the commission. We will be tabling thousands more when the commission reconvenes. We have committed to do this and we certainly will do it.
The only admission I have not heard is an admission from them yesterday that they were wrong when they said that we had not tabled the CANMET report. In fact, as their own commission's counsel said today, not only did we table it but they received it months ago. They apologized for making the mistake, but no apologies from the hon. members opposite.

Mr. Speaker, I want to come back to this minister or the acting minister.
I think they both understand that in a mining accident of this severity where lives were lost and safety was compromised, any government or agency involved has the utmost responsibility for accountability.
Ten months ago the government was asked to produce all the documents. It did not do that. It has withheld a key document outlining the federal role in the funding of the Westray mine incident. Even now with the threat of a federal commission of inquiry the minister still says: "Well, we may or may not put it forward. We haven't put it forward". They rejected, stonewalled, stopped the opposition.
Who made that decision? Was it this minister? Was it the Prime Minister? Was it the former Minister of Justice? Was it the minister of energy? Who is responsible for the cover-up?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only cover-up the House has heard in the last two days is material that the hon. member's colleagues had yesterday that they kept to themselves for three or four months. It affects the lives of these 26 miners. If they cared about it, why did they not release it before yesterday?
The other point is that the hon. member makes the premise that there was a safety problem. We do not know. That is why the commission was struck by the provincial government, to look into whether there was a safety problem and, if so, who was the cause of it, what was the cause of it.
We want to co-operate with that. It is provincial jurisdiction. It is a provincial inquiry. We are going to co-operate fully with them as we have in the past and will in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism.
Eleven days after the blast that killed 26 men at Westray the minister said in this House, and I quote him: "These Westray documents are coming together very quickly. I hope that we will be able to get them before the public shortly". That is what he said.
As we know nothing has been put before the public, although we do have a document with everything wiped out, censored, except the title and we have another one that was obviously censored by some Tory in a back room.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Order. Withdraw.
What I want to ask the minister is this. When will he release untampered documents-
Order.
-so that the Canadian people can see if the Prime Minister is interested in miner safety or the careers of his justice minister and his good buddy, Donny Cameron?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member makes two mistakes. First of all he is politicizing in a very big way what is basically a human

Oral Questions
tragedy. Second, he has failed to do his homework. He has failed to do 7,000 pages worth of homework. We have already tabled 7,000 pages on this subject and we have thousands more to come when the commission reconvenes.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows politics is written all over this one. That is the point he is trying to skate around.
My colleague, the House leader, wrote the government just four days after the tragedy advocating that every document which may touch directly or indirectly on the Westray case be preserved and protected. Now a federal judge tells us that the federal Department of Justice had deliberately and consistently withheld information about Westray from the provincial inquiry and that documents had been censored and altered in back rooms.
My question is for the Minister of Justice. Why did he or his predecessor think it necessary on this case to muddy the waters, to fudge the record?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the party opposite are having a terrible time listening to my answers. They are having a terrible time dealing with what I have already told them: not only have we co-operated with the commission fully but also the allegation he just made is patently false.
Let me read again the letter that I have just received from the commission counsel. It states:
I can confirm to you that the report identified by our file 1ST 9 is the document which is being referred to as the "CanMet" Report and that it was received from your client as part of the delivery of documents in June of 1992.
The hon. members opposite said we never sent the report or if we had sent it we only sent part of it. The commission counsel is now saying they were wrong and we were right.
opposition is confused, we are confused, and the public is confused.
We have to get something straight. Yesterday the commission counsel for the inquiry said in a prepared release that the document they had called the CANMET report was not supplied by the government.
Today the minister quotes a letter, part of which reads:
In the Fall of 1992, we became aware of a document identified as a "CanMet" Report. On checking our documents, we found no reference to CanMet. We subsequently obtained a copy of a Report from another source which had a title page identifying it as "CANMET REVIEW".
The person who supplied the report to the commission of inquiry in Nova Scotia was Alexa McDonough, the NDP leader of the party in Nova Scotia, not the federal government. We have that from two independent sources within the commission.
I ask the minister to finally try to get the answers straight. Did the government supply the report to the commission or not? What report did it supply? When are we going to get to the truth of this matter? Will he table his letter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed with the tone of my hon. friend's question. His party, to some degree, has not played politics with this issue as the Liberals have. Now he is doing that by mentioning names of prominent political people in the provincial legislature.
Let me tell the member this. If he reads this letter, and I invite him to read the letter, the commission counsel is saying that the reason they made the mistake is they did not get the title right. They now admit they had the document all along and they apologized for it. If the hon. member wants me to read all five paragraphs of the letter I will be glad to do it.

Mr. Speaker, to begin with I thought the usual practice in this place was for a minister, when he read from correspondence, to immediately table that correspondence. Since he has not yet done so I hope he will very soon.

The last thing I want to do is play politics with this
Mr. Speaker, the only thing certain about this whole issue, especially since 26 lives were lost. As I stated Westray episode is that the government is confused, the before, on a very brief supplementary, there is a lot of

March 31, 1993
Oral Questions
confusion and most of all the confusion is among the public, the miners and the people of Nova Scotia.
Last June my colleague from Edmonton East asked the minister that in view of the fact he agreed the commission of inquiry had no power to compel the federal government to supply documents and seeing as that has become one of the most uncertain and confusing issues in this whole affair, will the minister and the government now agree to hold a federal inquiry that will have powers so we can get at the truth? The government has the power to seek and demand the truth. Can we get this matter clarified, put politics aside and get safety in the mines of Nova Scotia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member needs a reality check again.
What we have here is a provincial inquiry into a matter of provincial jurisdiction which is safety. Regulation of safety in mines has always been provincial. That is why, in fact, the provincial government quite properly is having an inquiry. We want to co-operate because I believe the commission can get to the bottom of this. We have already sent them 7,000 documents. We will be sending them thousands more when they reconvene.
Not only that, but the federal government's role in this was simply as a loan guarantor. This is very far from safety in mining, but as a loan guarantor we want to participate fully in the inquiry. We look forward to co-operating with the commission.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Supply and Services or whoever answers for him.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-115 is the implementing legislation for the North American free trade agreement. NAFTA, as it is otherwise known, is a major development in Canadian political and economic history
March 31, 1993

by anyone's standards, regardless of their view on the matter, and needs to be debated adequately in the Elouse of Commons, especially at second reading where the principle of the issue is to be debated. To dispose of second reading after only a few hours of parliamentary debate last Thursday and today is clearly an abomination.
As you said on April 14, 1987:
It is essential to our democratic system that controversial issues should be debated at reasonable length so that every reasonable opportunity shall be available to hear the arguments pro and con and that reasonable delaying tactics should be permissible to enable opponents of a measure to enlist public support for their point of view.
NAFTA is certainly a controversial issue and should therefore be debated at reasonable length. It is, as the Action Canada Network said in a press release this morning, an international treaty which Canadians, through their elected members of Parliament, must have an opportunity to analyse and debate in an open public forum.
In your decision of April 14, 1987 you said:
The fundamental rights of members can be violated by the tactics of obstruction as well as by the unreasonable restriction of debate.
I agree. On that occasion you were concerned about the deadlock that had been produced on Bill C-22 as a result of certain opposition tactics.
Today we are faced with the other danger to the fundamental rights of members that you correctly identified in that decision, an unreasonable restriction of debate. For if a day and a half at second reading on something like NAFTA is not unreasonable one has to ask the question: What would be called unreasonable? Would just a day be called unreasonable but a day and a half called reasonable? Both are an unreasonable restriction of debate and should not be tolerated. This is why we appeal to you as the guardian of the House, which you are, Mr. Speaker.
Since 1988 we have seen closure used 17 times, almost as many times as in the whole history of Parliament, and time allocation, which I am objecting to today, used even more often than that. Indeed, thanks to the unilateral changes in the rules of the House in April 1991, time
Government Orders
allocation, which used to be regarded as the more moderate way of limiting debate, is now more convenient and easy for the government than closure itself, and the practice of using time allocation has accordingly become more attractive.
Surely there is a limit, a line beyond which the rights and responsibilities of Parliament itself are abrogated when important issues are immediately time allocated, without the opposition having time to debate such crucial issues and to take whatever political responsibility there may be for a certain amount of delay. The expectation of the Canadian people is that time allocation is something that governments enact in exasperation over a prolonged debate, not after a day and a half.
To enact time allocation without even allowing a reasonable debate on NAFTA violates every legitimate perception of how Parliament should work and the occasional need for governments to bring an end to debate.
I am fully aware that I am asking you to do something out of the ordinary, something new. But you are a new Speaker, new in the sense that you are the first to be elected by the whole House by secret ballot. You are a creature and servant of the House in a way that no previous Canadian Speaker has ever been, no matter how good previous Speakers may have been in their own right. You have the authority, I believe, if you choose to use it, to do what might otherwise be seen as unacceptable, at least by some.
The situation cries out for your intervention. Indeed, as you said yourself, in the decision of April 14, 1987: "there comes a time when the Chair has to face its responsibilities" and permit what in previous circumstances might have been ruled unacceptable by modifying or varying an earlier decision. I might add here, modifying or varying an earlier tradition.
An eminent parliamentary authority, Josef Redlich, which you have quoted yourself on occasion, has said that it is the duty of the Speaker to serve the majority and the minority "by maintaining the rules and the usage of centuries and by taking care that both majority and minority are not impeded in the use of the forces and the weapons which the order of business provides for the

Government Orders
strong and the weak. Protection of a majority against obstruction and protection of a minority against oppression are both alike functions of the Chair".
In Parliament, as it now stands, the opposition is perpetually and chronically weak thanks to the unilateral rule changes brought in, in April 1991, and protection of the minority against oppression should now be your major concern. I submit to you that this time allocation motion is just that kind of oppression which you need to protect the minority from.
Mr. Speaker, in 1987 you asked the question reflecting on the manner in which you were elected as to whether or not the House of Commons had matured "enough to confer upon its presiding officer the discretionary powers necessary to control abuse and resolve deadlocks that the British House of Commons gave its Speaker over a century ago". You said then that you believed the Canadian House of Commons had matured to that point. On that basis you acted to break the deadlock.
I now ask you to act on the same basis to control abuse in a Parliament that has seen more time allocation in which the opposition is weaker and in which the idea of giving the Speaker such discretion has come into its own. Indeed, a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on House Management recently recommended to the full committee that such discretion on the part of the Speaker be part of the full committee's report to the House on parliamentary reform that could be tabled any day now.
There is a recognition that with increased government powers must come some other form of checking abuses of power. This checking mechanism used to be the role of the opposition but which is no more thanks to the rule changes that I mentioned before.
The time allocation now before us on NAFTA is in my judgment and that of my colleagues just the sort of situation in which the Speaker's role is crucial. Indeed, if this is not the kind of situation that demands the intervention of the Chair, it is hard to imagine what would be and therefore what meaning there might be in having the Speaker exercise such discretion.
Mr. Speaker, Parliament is in your hands. On April 14 you said: "Notice of time allocation motions after only a few hours of debate at any stage of a bill can also be an
abuse". This is exactly what we have before us this afternoon. If the North American free trade agreement can be rushed through the House of Commons with just two days' debate then Canadians will have just cause to despair about their Parliament as a place where important issues are adequately debated. We in the NDP caucus call on you to exercise your discretion and refuse to entertain, or to call the vote, on the time allocation motion on Bill C-115 until you are satisfied that there has been adequate debate on second reading.
Finally, I appeal to that which you have often appealed to yourself, and that is common sense. It is that profound sense, as you once described it, of what is appropriate under certain circumstances and what is acceptable to reasonable people.
May I ask that at the very least, given what I believe to be the historic significance of the judgment you are being called upon to make not in terms of the North American free trade agreement but in terms of Parliament, that you take whatever time is necessary to reflect on the issue before you and ask the government to withdraw its motion until you have had ample time to consider the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my distinguished colleague, the Minister for International Trade, before this House and throughout this nation has made a solid case for the North American Free Trade Agreement. It is the vision and the courage of the Prime Minister, and that of my colleague the Minister for International Trade, and all in our government, that has opened a bold opportunity and a new window for Canada in this hemisphere.

Let me say at the outset that it is regrettable that our friends on the other side, especially the NDP members, use every trick in the book to try to prevent debate on the real substantial issue of the North American free trade agreement.
I saw last week and earlier today where time was lost on procedural arguments instead of debating the substance about which I am sure Canadians want to hear, that is the NAFTA agreement itself.
This agreement will allow all Canadians to realize the rich potential of the world's largest trading market. It will further a regional alliance which shall grow even further in the future, to include other nations, serving our national interests and those of all others in this hemisphere and all in the global trading system.
Over the last eight years, our government has taken the right steps at the right time, from the outset of our mandate in 1984 to lay the foundations for economic growth. Inflation is beaten back, interest rates are at a 20-year low, exports are surging, and business has become increasingly competitive with our access to the global marketplace. And now we are taking one more step forward in a consistent, coherent, and, yes, courageous way with the North American Free Trade Agreement.
NAFTA will help us improve our economy in two ways: it will create more new and high paying jobs here than any low wage jobs it costs, and it will protect Canada's place in the U.S. marketplace, our most important customer. I especially rise in this debate to address the issue of labour adjustment. That question has become the focus of a great deal of attention, in some ways sidelining other issues which are also of great importance. As Minister of Employment and Immigration, I am aware of the tragedy of unemployment, and the personal trauma of finding that technology has made
March 31, 1993

obsolete the hard-earned skills which served workers well in another era and generation.
Now technology and knowledge are replacing traditional industries as the building blocks of prosperity. You hear it everywhere, but it is a reality. Since the industrial revolution, old technologies and infrastructure have been forced aside by new technologies and the opening up of new markets.
Some industries decline, while others emerge as growth generators. As this happens, we see unemployment of displaced workers while employers in the new sectors complain they cannot find enough workers with the necessary skills. This is not a new phenomenon. The only difference today is that the change of pace has picked up dramatically.
By the year 2000, almost half of all new jobs will require more than five years of education and training beyond high school. Highly educated workers will be at a premium. These highly productive workers will receive high wages.
That is what we should be preparing ourselves for.
We should not be worrying about lower paying jobs moving to Mexico, because Mexico has not moved as rapidly along the path of development and industrial change as has Canada.

There is only one way to compete in this new age for jobs or business, and that is through learning, education, training, skills development and entrepreneurship on a lifelong, never stop basis.
Our economic success depends first and foremost on the cutting edge skills and forward thinking attitudes which people bring to the work place. We use technology to improve productivity. We have to be sure we have guaranteed access to a growing market for our goods and services.
As the world is forming trading blocs, access we have counted on in the past may not always be there. It only makes sense to reject the pleas of those who lack confidence in Canada and its workers, to put ourselves in a position to seize this unique moment and to move forward.
Government Orders
I am not saying NAFTA will not require changes in the way we do business in Canada, but I echo the sentiments expressed in the report of the Economic Policy Council of the United Nations Association of the United States. That distinguished labour-business forum explores the implications for business and labour on an increasingly interdependent world economy.
Its report entitled The Social Implication of the North American Free Trade Agreement states: "NAFTA will be only one of many factors causing structural change in the economy". I agree with that, and that is why I also concur with the EPC in opposing the creation of special NAFTA adjustment programs.

Moreover, the report urges consolidating existing adjustment programs as well as expanding these programs to cover most displaced workers. It points out that only a small fraction of eligible workers benefits from these programs today.
It says that adjustment assistance should provide health benefits and enough income support to enable displaced workers to enter retraining programs.
Finally, it recommends only business-labour certified retraining programs be eligible for government subsidy. Long before NAFTA was on the horizon, we began to make a number of moves in response to recommendations of the Advisory Council on Adjustment headed by Mr. Jean de Grandpre.

The Labour Force Development Strategy was established in part to respond to the key recommendations of the de Grandpre commission. One of the most significant moves was to begin the shift away from using our now $20 billion plus a year unemployment insurance program as a passive income assistance system to a more active investment program to access employment and training.
We must continue to move in this direction using all our social programs to empower people with solutions, knowledge and choices.
We talk about the need to create an opportunity society that offers the chance to be productive at every stage of every person's life. We are already dedicating vast resources which could be reoriented in this way. Our UI program is more comprehensive and generous than

March 31, 1993
Government Orders
that offered in the United States, and 80 per cent of Canada's unemployed workers receive benefits as compared to 35 per cent in the United States. We spend three and a half times more on UI per capita than the United States. Government spending on training in Canada is twice that of the United States.
We now need to lever Canadian employers to increase training expenditures by dramatic proportions to at least match U.S. private sector levels.
The Canada Labour Force Development Board and regional and local boards are beginning, in partnership, to strongly encourage private sector training. In 1993-94 the government will spend $3.8 billion on labour market programs. That is 80 per cent more than we were spending in 1989-90. Training and adjustment, supported by the UI program in 1993, will account for $2.21 billion, four and half times the 1990 level.
We have a way to go. Canada is still spending more per capita on passive labour market measures than any other G-7 country. We rank 15th among all OECD countries.
Through our national sectoral human resources planning initiative we are furthering partnerships of workers, employers and other stakeholders to develop comprehensive development strategies. Over two million workers in Canada are benefiting from more than 900 planning agreements.
We are also implementing a new initiative aimed at providing training opportunities for workers with a demonstrated longer term attachment to the labour force. That is a first in Canada. No government has ever targeted these displaced workers to give them the kind of tailored programming assistance they need to reintegrate into the labour market. Of course no one on the other side wants to talk about these initiatives for longer term attachment of people to the labour force.
We have a program to promote the swift reintegration into the work force of workers displaced by economic changes of any kind. For non-UI recipients we have the Canadian Jobs Strategy which spent $1.6 billion to
provide a wide range of services to help Canadians enhance their employability.

In short, we are using new skills, innovative approaches and new dollars so workers can rebound quickly and liberate their own potential, rather than creating safety nets which trap for life so many of those who land in them lost to the numbing grip of dependency. There could be nothing we could regret more than to let the NAFTA opportunity founder and then watch Canada sink behind, cut off from the potentially explosive growth of the nations of Latin America.
I invite my hon. friends, the members opposite, to reject short term political considerations, to reject appeals to unfounded fears, to face squarely the reality and opportunity of these times.
Join with the government in taking credit for having supported a progressive trade agreement which enhances the future for all workers, all Canadians.
On March 28 The Toronto Star quoted the hon. Leader of the NDP as calling for members to "kick butt" in opposing NAFTA. Honourable members will know that this is not the kind of language I usually choose to use, but if that be her call and those of her fellow travellers- the Maude Barlows and Bob Whites, et al-I suggest they have chosen the wrong butt.
Targeting the FTA and now NAFTA may gain a quick sound bite and a fleeting image of commitment to the unemployed or those fearful of losing jobs, but the evidence is simply not there to support these wild allegations.
I remember that Canadians heard during the 1988 election campaign prophets of doom who used absolutely every possible means to scare people in the different regions of the country, and particularly in my province of New Brunswick and in all of Atlantic Canada, among other things telling our seniors that they would lose their social safety net, predicting the sale of schools to Americans, telling people back home that their children would be drafted by the American army. It was unbelievable. Now they are at it again, trying to scare Canadians with the North American Free Trade Agreement.
March 31, 1993

Engaging in a phoney war in an attempt ot make political hay on misplaced fears and insecurities will back fire in the face of the facts and the only thing that will get butted, to use the expression of the NDP leader, is the purveyors of such distorted logic.
The window of opportunity today is momentarily open. Let us go ahead and use the solid agreement that we have, as well as the assurance and the confidence flowing from this new trilateral partnership, and also our own strength and our own ability as Canadians to face new challenges as well or better than anyone else in the world.
My colleague, the Minister for International Trade, demonstrated on several occasions in this House that the economic recovery and the current growth are the results of our exports. Yet these people would still want to isolate Canada, put up smoke-screens around our country and keep us here because, according to them, we are not good enough to be competitive.

We are not good enough to compete. We are not trained enough. We are not trainable. We should stay here. The island of Canada should close itself to the world. That message of our friends on the other side is a great misunderstanding of the Canadian population.
Canadians are a hard working people who have faced many challenges in the past. We were able to meet those challenges because we were there. We did not shy away from the challenge. I know that for business, labour and all those communities across Canada that want to move forward the North American free trade agreement will be a great success.

Madam Speaker, let me say first that if this was not such a sad and shameful day in the history of this country I would be amused by the hon. minister's remarks.

They are thrilled at the opportunities being
Government Orders
provided by this government under the free trade agreements".
The fact of the matter is there is not a household in this country that has not been severely injured and hurt by the policies of this government. It is the highest unemployment rate in the OECD world. Of course the problem is that we have ministers of the Crown who do not understand that. They never talk about it. It does not exist for them. What did the minister say? He said: "It is a smoke-screen out there".
There is no understanding of the real issue which is that people want to work. They want to do so with a certain sense of dignity and honour. This is what the debate is really about. It is giving those people a voice, tiying as hard as we might to ensure they can be heard and to break through the wall and cloak of silence that has been put upon them by this government.
Madam Speaker, do you realize that with the vote this afternoon closure has been used in this House 25 times since 1988? That equals the number of times closure was used from 1913 to 1988. In four years this government has used closure more often than all the other governments going back to 1913.
That is a direct demonstration of the kind of disdain the Minister for International Trade and his colleagues have for the Canadian people. They do not want to give them a chance to be heard. They do not want to hear a dialogue or a debate. They simply want to close the door so that they cannot hear the real voice of the Canadian people. The real voice is saying that these kinds of arrangements concocted in the back rooms, in the wealthy eating clubs the Minister for International Trade frequents, are not working in the interest of Canadians. They are not working in the interests of other working people around this continent.
I found it interesting when I went back and read the remarks of the trade minister. It was fascinating how he attempted with all the skill of his public relations manipulators to try to put a gloss on what has been taking place. He said that exports in 1992 reached a record high of $157 billion. What he did not say was that imports also reached a record high. In fact our global trade surplus in 1992 is the smallest going back to 1981.

Government Orders
Our trade surplus in 1982-this minister loves to talk about the difficult times of 1982-was $17.7 billion. The trade surplus last year was $9.5 billion. Let us look at some other figures. The real imbalance-
You did not take the time to debate the matter.
Oh, the thin skin of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Madam Speaker. I wish to caution my friend. We are talking about the NAFTA. He is using figures that relate to our total trade and not to the Canada-U.S. trade. If he used the Canada-U.S. trade figures he would know quite clearly that-
That is debate and not a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the hon. members on my left will want at least to let me hear a sentence before declaring that it is not a point of order.
Probably the hon. minister will want to take the opportunity of question or comments to rise and put on the record whatever he wants on the record.

Madam Speaker, I hope you will not include the time taken up in this frivolous intervention of the thin-skinned minister who cannot stand to hear the truth as it comes out in this House.
Let us deal with something he talked about in the United States. Let me just go back to the figures from Statistics Canada that relate to our trade with the United States.
Our cumulative trade surplus for the four years before the free trade agreement was $69.1 billion, which was 14 per cent higher than the four years after the free trade agreement. Here is the minister saying what a great accomplishment it is, but the fact of the matter is that our trade surplus is far less after 1988 and the free trade agreement than it was before.
The minister is leaving the House. We now finally have won the debate and he retreats from the field because he cannot stand the heat. He cannot stand the heat because he knows that the figures provided by the agency of the government, Statistics Canada, totally refute the absolute nonsensical figures that he has tried to display in this House during this debate. He is certainly a stranger to the truth, a stranger indeed.
The minister tries to suggest that the global trade surplus does not matter somehow. What he does not want to recognize or acknowledge is that since the free trade agreement we have run a decline or a net deficit with every other trading area of the world except the United States. He has forgotten that Canada as a nation of international traders must have a diversified trade base. We must trade with the Pacific Rim, Europe, Central America and Latin America, but the fact of the matter is that our trade is going down with the rest of the world.
We have less of a surplus with the United States. Our trade is going down around the world and we have a Minister for International Trade who walks around with rose-coloured glasses and says that things have never been rosier and things have never been better.
Try telling that to 1.6 million Canadians because they are the living evidence of just how wrong this trade policy has become. The reason this government has used closure 25 times-more than in the entire history of Parliament-in the last four years is that it is the only way it can use its bludgeoning majority to get its neo-Conservative legislation through this House. It knows the Canadian people will not stand for it otherwise. Just like the minister who retreats from the House, it cannot stand the heat. It cannot stand the truth. It cannot stand to deal with the real facts.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Please, the minister is in the House.

He is sitting in the back row, a position he will be occupying for the next four years once the election is called. He is just practising. It is also important to point out something very important. This example of misuse of figures is an attempt to use the propaganda machine of the government to mislead Canadians. It is another example of how
March 31, 1993

the NAFTA bill is really used to masquerade the kind of programs that only this government is left implementing.
Around the world governments are changing because they realize there has to be a more activist, public minded, public interest form of government. Their cronies in the old administration in the United States have now been booted out, which will soon happen here. That is the reason the government is rushing the legislation through. That is the reason we are into this crazy acceleration of legislation when the other partners to the agreement have not even begun to look at it yet.
Is it not interesting, is it not fascinating that the present U.S. administration said that it must begin to look seriously at questions dealing with labour standards and environmental standards to protect the interests of American workers, American plants and American businesses? Our own government is not prepared to stand and say the same for Canadians. It is not prepared to get up and say that it also thinks there should be serious safeguards on labour, serious safeguards on the environment, serious safeguards against the countervail duties and the harassment by the United States.
It says there is no need to think about changes. It is all driven by that maniacal desire to get this legislation through as the last cornerstone in the crown of this discredited Prime Minister, who is being booted out by public opinion in Canada because he is afraid to stand and take the heat just as the Minister for International Trade is afraid to take the heat.
What we are putting in jeopardy and danger once again are the interests of Canadians because we have no policy and no program to make sure they are properly incorporated in these trading arrangements.
What further evidence do we need than the kind of information now coming out in the United States on the question of the drug patent law? A senior senator of the United States, David Pryor from Oklahoma, has written to his trade representative and said they should not do NAFTA because within NAFTA are prohibitions to bringing in compulsory licensing arrangements that will allow them to keep our drug prices at a respectable modest rate.
Yet within this NAFTA bill Canada, which already has compulsory licensing, is taking it out. We see a report in today's paper that Canada presently leads the world in
Government Orders
high cost drugs in 40 to 100 items. Is that something to be proud of?
I want to say this to members opposite. Are they really pleased when they go back into their ridings and speak to the seniors who have to use more drugs? Are they pleased when they speak to people on lower incomes who have to pay more for drugs? Because of this legislation, because of their initiative, they are now forcing people to pay prices which are the highest in the world.
Government members are going to vote for a bill that will entrench that in an international agreement so that a future government, a few months from now after the election, is going to find it more difficult to renegotiate. They are going to rush it through and hammer it through by means of closure and time allocation. Is that something that they can be proud of? Do they want to put in their householders that drug prices have escalated by 30 per cent or by 40 per cent and that they are going to entrench and prohibit any remedial action even though our partners in the United States are saying they had better start doing the same thing?
Senator Pryor is saying to the trade representative, do not sign the agreement the way it is because it will prohibit us from bringing in the kind of measures that the Canadians used to have. What a strange way of turning logic, truth and rationality on its head. What a terrible transgression this government is committing against the people of this country by pushing through this bill without any consideration of their interests.
It is fascinating watching the Tory leadership campaign. They are all out there saying they must bring down the cost of government and health care has to be amended, so let us bring in user fees. Yet by this very action alone, the vote they are going to take tonight on NAFTA, they will be pushing up drug prices and therefore causing every health care scheme in every single province in this country to pay 10 per cent to 15 per cent more.
Yet these are the same people, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of the Environment, who are out there with all the fervour at their command saying they have to do something about health costs. The most important thing we could do about health costs is defeat this bill and defeat this government so we can at

March 31, 1993
Government Orders
least keep drug costs down and not have them escalating to $300 million, $400 million or $500 million a year.
What a terrible travesty of justice and truth is being committed. How can anybody take this new politics seriously? The new politics is simply a smoke-screen for the old slimy, sleazy way of dragging and pushing people into the ground. That is what this bill is all about. Those members on the government side who have a scintilla of integrity left have only one choice, and that is to vote against this bill for the sake of the people in their own ridings.
The people opposite, and I heard the Minister of Employment and Immigration, like to say that they think Canadians can be competitive, they think we can run globally, and it is the other side who is trying to be protectionist. Not so, that is not the case at all. Mr. Speaker, do you know what this bill also does? Do you know what is contained in NAFTA? There are a number of discriminatory clauses in the NAFTA bill that prohibit and set up discriminatory clauses against other countries with whom we want to do business.
I come from western Canada. We are now beginning to do more trade with the Pacific Rim than with the United States. Yet it was not so long ago when I was on a trip to Japan and met with senior officials of the Japanese government who said to me directly that in the NAFTA arrangement there are at least five or six major areas that discriminate against other countries. We are trying to diversify our trade at a time when the world is changing so rapidly, with so many opportunities out there to trade with a wide variety of countries, and what are we doing? This government is bringing in a bill that builds a wall around the continent and sets up discriminatory trade arrangements.
I will explain what the result will be. This kind of trade bloc mentality will force other regions of the world to do the same. We will end up with a war between trading blocs, which is the worst kind of circumstance that we could possibly have.
Textiles, financial services, banking, and content rules all basically say to other trading partners in the Pacific Rim that they are not as equal as the Americans or the Mexicans. How do we go and present ourselves as an honest, open international trader when we are discriminating against those potential trading partners?
Contrary to the arguments, we are trying to say that the future of this country does lie in an international trading arena and in making sure there are fair, open trading rules that apply equally to all countries. We should not set up discriminatory trading blocs that compete with one another. As Canadians we should be looking to the wide world so we will not suffer the kind of trade decline in which we have a net decline with every other trading region in the world and our trade is decreasing.
That is why we have said time and again, we said it during the debate on the free trade agreement and we say it now, that the most important trading arrangement that Canada belongs to is the General Agreement on Trades and Thrifts. It is an international agreement. It sets out rules that apply to everybody equally. It has a dispute settlement system that is based upon a definition of subsidy that is not unilaterally decided by one country, as it is under the FTA. It resulted in Canada being able to lower tariff barriers, to escape from the kind of harassment that we have had for the past four years, and to ensure that there is equal treatment for north, south, east and west and countries around the world.
I cannot and would not want to represent the views of the NDP but I can tell you what are the views of this party. We are true international traders. We believe that the future of this country exists in broadening, diversifying and opening up all kinds of new trade options. One of the reasons why NAFTA does not fit the bill is because it closes off options and replaces the GATT with a regime that is not nearly as good. It sets up, as we have just seen with the drug patent law, prohibitions and restrictions on the rights of Canadians that do not exist under the GATT.
The true protectionists are these continentalists across from us who are trying to draw the Canadian trading option into one region, one area, one place and forgo the opportunities that exist around the world.
The real secret to Canadian economic prosperity, to recreating the opportunity for jobs and growth and development is to see a horizon that circumvents the entire globe, that sees the opportunities in the Americas, not through the kind of agreement that restricts but one
March 31, 1993

that takes in the entire hemisphere, that opens up our opportunities in the Pacific Rim where we want to be honest, open and fair traders and not discriminate against them.
That is the real choice for Canadians. That is the choice that will be coming from the electorate. I say that NAFTA will not be a fait accompli because the Americans are not going to complete it by then. The only country that is having it rammed through its legislature is this country by this government. The rest of them recognize that their own people need time for debate, time for dialogue, time for proper examination. That is what we want Canadians to have. We think that if we had that time and that opportunity, we would have a trading policy and a trading strategy which would give Canadians that opening to the world we so desperately need.

Nothing in NAFTA is going to prevent the initiatives that the government has taken to increase trade in Asia, the Caribbean and in other parts of the world.
I say to him, very simply, we know where this party stands; four square behind NAFTA. We know where the NDP stand; totally against it. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I guess that is a question.

That goes back to the Canada-U.S. auto pact which our government negotiated way

back when. It was not affected by the free trade agreement, by the acknowledgement of their own errors.
