Mr. Speaker, it will be a comment with a brief question.
I would like to give the House the benefit of what is happening in Chesterville in the riding of Stormont- Dundas presently which I think is very relevant to today's debate.
Nestle Canada has a plant located at Chesterville in my riding of Stormont-Dundas. Last Saturday the company locked out its production line workers, 220 of them, after their union rejected a proposed contract offer from the company which included a continental work week.
The company states that its employees must accept a continental work week and give up premium pay for working on weekends if the plant is to be competitive in the North American marketplace.
The Chesterville plant exports 70 per cent of its products to the U.S. and it faces competition from other Nestle plants both in the U.S. and Mexico. In addition, those products made in Mexico are usually cheaper to produce, given the much lower wages paid to their employees there.
The Nestle situation is an indication of what is to come for Canadian workers if NAFTA goes ahead without any safeguards to protect Canadian workers. The current recession has crippled the Canadian industry. The Cana-da-U.S. free trade deal has taken its toll and now our workers will have to face NAFTA.
Workers at Chesterville are being told that unless they accept significant changes to their work schedules and give up weekend pay rates, they will not be able to compete with their own plants in the U.S. and Mexico.
It is obvious that with the precarious state of North American trade and the inequality that exists within free trade deals like NAFTA, companies like Nestle have no choice but to pit one of their own plants against other plants of their own.
For Canadian plants this means paring down employee wages, benefits and working conditions. Moreover, no matter what happens, it is highly unlikely that Canadian plants like Chesterville will ever have the opportunity to compete on a level playing field with plants in Mexico, given the low salaries and lack of benefits provided to workers there.
I want to ask my hon. colleague, the member for Winnipeg South Centre, if he can explain why the present government is pursuing NAFTA with such a vengeance and why the government is enforcing time allocation, forcing a vote on second reading of Bill C-115 today.

Mr. Speaker, your generosity is much appreciated.
I say to my colleague from Stormont-Dundas that we should not be surprised if the government uses closure on this bill because it has used it 25 times since 1988. It has used it more often in the last four years than it had been used in the previous 70 or 80 years.
It has become a way of life. They are narcotic. They know that they cannot take the heat and the pressure of an ordinary proper political dialogue in the Parliament of Canada so they shut the place down. They use it like a hammer to bludgeon Canadians into accepting without any opportunity for a response.
I want to say to the hon. member that I think he makes a very important point about what happened in his riding.
It is a point that all members of this party have been making unanimously, with one voice. We need to renegotiate this agreement. We need to find ways of ensuring that this kind of disparity in labour and environmental standards will not be used to provide for major transferences of companies from one area to another.
The companies will not have that kind of sink-hole to use to say: "We will move to a place where we do not have to make sure the water is clean, the air is fresh or that the workers get proper protection. We will go where anything goes".
You would have thought after the horrible experience of the free trade agreement when we had a haemorrhaging of jobs across the border that the government would
March 31, 1993

have taken the opportunity offered to it by the Clinton administration to do the same thing.
Instead, the minister of trade gets up and says to the Prime Minister: "It is not in our interest to do that". No. They define their interests narrowly according to the very small group of power brokers who run this party across from us. They are dictating the economic life of this country. They do not understand that there is a broad range of Canadians out there who also have some rights, the right to prosper and the right to have a job.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak for a short time on the objectives and overview of NAFTA.
On August 12, after 14 months of negotiations, Canada reached agreement with the United States and Mexico on the North American free trade agreement.
This trade agreement creates the world's largest free trade zone. Contrary to what the opposition would have Canadians believe, it will make Canada more competitive and help secure Canada's prosperity.
Canada could ill afford to be excluded from a free trade agreement within the United States and Mexico. Some say we should have stayed away from the table, ignored what was going on around us, buried our heads in the sand. I ask these people, would our interests be served by letting the United States and Mexico go it alone? They would not and Canadians know this.
Canadians do not stand still and watch the world go by as some people would have us do. No. Canadians protect their interests, pursue opportunities and rise to new challenges.
Some say involving Canada in the North American free trade agreement comes at the price of missing other opportunities to expand our exports. This is simply not true. Quite the contrary. Participation in NAFTA extends and improves these opportunities. By competing successfully in an expanded and dynamic North American market, Canadian companies will be better positioned to compete in the markets around the world.
The NAFTA goes to the heart of Canada's fundamental interests as a nation that depends on trade. If Canadians did not sell the goods and services we produce at home to buyers in other countries, one out of every
Government Orders
four Canadian jobs would disappear. It is as simple as that.
Canada got involved in the NAFTA to protect those interests and to take advantage of opportunities that will strengthen our global trading position. Globalization is something we have been hearing about for a while now. While it has become something of a buzzword its meaning is quite clear. Simply put, globalization describes emerging production and marketing techniques that take advantage of the best of the world. For example, a single aeroplane may be designed by engineers in the United States and Germany, use parts made in Ontario and Korea, be financed by banks from Tokyo and London and be marketed around the world.
By participating in the NAFTA Canada is signalling its willingness to take advantage of globalization. The NAFTA shows we are willing to continue changing and it shows we are looking to the future, ready to face the challenges and opportunities presented by the new economic climate in Mexico.
The North American free trade agreement will benefit all three participating countries by increasing trade and prosperity. In particular, the NAFTA will help the Mexican economy develop. It will allow Mexico to attract investment and it will provide new opportunities for the Mexican people.
The NAFTA ensures that Canadian knowledge and expertise will help Mexico achieve a higher standard of living while increasing Canada's own export trade.
The fuller integration of Mexico into the North American economy will reinforce economic, trade, monetary and fiscal reforms already undertaken by Mexico. This will result in a more prosperous Mexico, a Mexico better able to manage its debt and in a better position to import Canadian goods and services.
Mexico offers a market of over 85 million consumers. As Mexico's economy expands and its prosperity grows, so will its demand for increasingly sophisticated imports.
When we told Canadians we would participate in the NAFTA negotiations we set out three objectives: better access for Canadian goods and services to Mexico; strengthening the benefits of the Canada-U.S. free

March 31, 1993
Government Orders
trade agreement; and improving our access to the world's single richest country. This guarantees Canada's status as a highly desirable location for investors to serve the North American market. We met these objectives, each one. What we did in the NAFTA is what we said we would do all along.
Mexico is one of the fastest growing and most promising markets in the world. But in the past it has been a very difficult market for Canadians to penetrate. When Canada got the opportunity to secure access for our exporters it was only logical to pursue it.
NAFTA removes the tariffs and other barriers which made selling to Mexico tough. As a result Canada now has guaranteed access to 85 million Mexican consumers and their growing spending power. This means benefits and new opportunities for Canadians and Canadian businesses from coast to coast.
When Canada got involved in the NAFTA we were determined to build on the benefits of the free trade agreement without giving up any of the advantages we already had and we did that.
The NAFTA clarifies rules of origin and improves customs operations. This will prevent any unilateral interpretation of trading rules such as what happened in the Honda dispute. As a matter of fact, the NAFTA resolves the problem we had with exports of the Honda Civics produced in Ontario.
The NAFTA covers many services that were not in the free trade agreement. It makes it easier for business people and professionals to travel for work to the United States. NAFTA enlarges the quotas for Canadian textiles and apparels shipped to the United States. The NAFTA strengthens and makes permanent the free trade agreement's dispute settlement mechanism so that Canadian exporters will get fair and unbiased treatment if they are the target of a trade complaint.
These and other improvements mean we now have an even better system to ensure that Canadian businesses can compete with those in the United States. And we did it while protecting important Canadian interests such as cultural industries, agricultural supply management, medicare, social programs and the environment. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I said the environment.
Since 1984 the Government of Canada has worked diligently with all sectors of the Canadian economy to renew and strengthen our economic position. The government undertook a plan that looked to the future rather than to the past. We were determined to confront the emerging global business environment and maintain our position as a leader in world trade.
New patterns were arising. Companies were not just doing business in different countries, they were spreading their operations across continents and around the world. This brought new challenges to Canada. If we could not be competitive there were plenty of other economies ready and waiting to do business.
The government saw these changes and realized it could do two things. If we ignored them, they were threats to the society that makes Canada the envy of the world, but if we accepted them and used them to our advantage they would ensure the future prosperity of all Canadians. Canadians are already part of the global economy.
As a nation Canada was founded on trade. Our success in selling goods and services to other countries has helped make Canada one of the wealthiest countries in the world. It has paid for infrastructure and social programs that are the envy of the globe.
Today our prosperity still depends on the sale abroad of more than 25 per cent of all we produce. As a country with a relatively small population, we must continually look beyond our own borders for new markets and opportunities. Success does not happen overnight. Building our competitiveness will be a painstaking process requiring concerted efforts from all sectors of our economy.
It will not be an easy task, but it is a vital one if Canada hopes to maintain its secure position in the global marketplace. It is a task we are confident of achieving by building partnerships with all sectors of the economy.
Canada has not been immune from the global recession. We have endured tough adjustment to technological development and to the globalization of production and market. But studies by independent organizations such as the University of Toronto indicate that the free trade agreement has helped stimulate growth, lowered the rate of inflation and cushioned the severity of the

recession in Canada. Without the free trade agreement the economic effects of the recession would have been much more severe.
The free trade agreement is providing Canadian business with the incentive to restructure, to prepare to meet global competition and to create the basis for our continued prosperity. The North American free trade agreement strengthens the foundation for global competition laid down in the free trade agreement.
Exporting is one of the main engines of growth and job creation in the Canadian economy. Exports account for one in four or over three million Canadian jobs. It is therefore essential that Canadians be able to compete effectively in international trade.
We guarantee our future not by running from global competition but by meeting it head on, by equipping ourselves to compete with the best by ensuring that we have in place the economic conditions needed to be competitive and by making world markets accessible to our products.
So the cornerstone of our plan was to ensure Canada became more competitive. This is happening. Lately Canada's productivity has seen remarkable gains and our ability to innovate and find smarter and better ways of doing business increases all the time.
Part of being competitive means having access to foreign markets and to be frank, it also means having to face competition. This is nothing to worry about because it will improve our performance. If you want an example, just take a look at the Olympic athletes. Any sprinter will tell you that the fastest times happen not in isolated practice sessions, but in the final heat when the world's best are racing side by side. By competing with other producers, Canada's industry will become better, stronger and more innovative.
I am confident that Canada can compete successfully in any arrangement that has fair and clear rules. That is what NAFTA is all about. By giving us access to foreign markets and establishing the rules of the game, NAFTA will help Canadians succeed and prosper in North America and around the world.

Mr. Speaker, everyone in this Chamber today will remember what I choose to call the great debate of 1988, when one
Government Orders
of the things that seemed to be at issue was that we were going to lose all of our water if we proceeded with the free trade agreement. You will remember that all of our water was going to be diverted. The Americans could hardly wait to get their hands on it. All of our rivers and lakes, we were going to pump it all down to California. Remember, within a few months it was going. We know what nonsense that was.
I wonder if I might ask my colleague who has just spoken if she has some thoughts on whether the North American free trade agreement will protect our water the same as the FTA protects our water, the same as the Canadian water policy protects our water.
We have had this raised in the last few days. Can we not put it to rest?

Thank you very much for the question. The large scale export of water is not covered in NAFTA and it is not covered in the free trade agreement. It never has been and never will be because that is not a good to be transported. It has never been an issue at the GATT and there is nothing to force Canada to construct a canal. Since we do not sell water now there are no terms which would be subject to dispute.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-115, the North American free trade agreement, is before this House today. Today also-

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend across the way for ceding the floor to me.
Four years ago when Canada entered the free trade agreement with the United States what we were actually doing was creating the largest bilateral trade relationship in the world.
Today there is clear evidence that the foresight shown by this government, and indeed it was foresight, has been of tremendous benefit to Canada. These benefits were confirmed in a study that was released by an independent group in October 1992. That group, the C.D. Howe

March 31, 1993
Government Orders
Institute, said that Canada's merchandise and service exports have thrived in most sectors that were liberalized under the FTA.
Canada has gained the most in exports of non-resource-based, high value-added manufacturing products to the U.S. These are the areas in which our future lies.
This government has taken the country out of its shell and has prepared it for the 21st century. All of the success has occurred during a world-wide recession. Just imagine what we can achieve during the recovery period in which we are now entering.
That is the reality of the situation. During a worldwide economic downturn Canadian exports to the U.S. grew not 1 per cent or 2 per cent and not even 9 per cent or 10 per cent, but nearly 20 per cent in the short time since the FTA has been in place.
Last year Canada enjoyed an all-time record in merchandise exports to the U.S. of $122.3 billion. In December 1992 the trade surplus-that is right, trade surplus-with the U.S. was $2 billion. That is an increase of over 26 per cent over the previous month.
Canada's exports to the U.S. even outperformed Japan. They are considered an economic powerhouse by eveiyone, even in the opposition, but Canada outperformed them and that is because of the FTA.
Like a great architect, this government knows that one must have a solid foundation before one can build a house. That is what the North American free trade agreement will do. It will add and build on the success of the FFA. It will not diminish what we have worked so hard to obtain but rather it will complement and strengthen what can be.
NAFTA incorporates many of the elements of the FTA and adds to them. Every decision in the deal is not perfect and we realize that in the end even politicians are human.
After four years of the FTA, the government identified certain mutually agreeable improvements and included them in the NAFTA. Each one of these went through the ultimate test: Will it benefit Canada? In every case the answer was a resounding yes. Some of the improvements that were made are the inclusion of fairer and more stable rules of origin, intellectual property rights, a significant expansion of the government's procurement opportunities and of course the inclusion of Mexico and giving Canada access to one of the fastest growing markets in the world.
When we entered into NAFTA talks in 1991 we had three broad objectives: first, to give Canada better access to the Mexican market; second, a trilateral agreement that would provide greater security for Canada's access to the U.S. market while maintaining the benefits that we achieved under the FTA; and third, it would be in Canada's interest if it preserved our status as a preferred location for investment. All of the objectives have been met.
The one thing that must be pointed out at the veiy beginning is that Mexico was already enjoying free trade with Canada but it was only one way. Roughly 80 per cent of Mexican products enter into Canada duty-free but Canadian exports to Mexico face an array of tariffs and other trade barriers. This is something many Canadians do not realize. They must know that the government was working for them to correct this imbalance, and we did.
As a result of the hard work undertaken by the trade minister and his staff Canada will be able to rebalance its trade with Mexico, especially in the automotive sector that is so very important to my province of Ontario.
Mexico has the fastest growing automobile market in North America. Due to the NAFTA Mexico will eliminate its protectionist auto policy, which has in the past restricted the importing of vehicles and forced parts and assembly operations to locate in Mexico, over a 10-year period.
This will go a long way in ensuring a viable future for the auto industry in Ontario. Evidence of this can be seen in the recent announcement by Chrysler Canada to put $600 million into its plants in Windsor, Ontario. If Chrysler believed the rhetoric that comes from the parties across the floor would it be investing $600 million in Ontario?
The auto industry and its workers are not the only winners in the NAITA. There is a virtual plethora of opportunities in a number of different sectors.
Ontario's machine producers will gain from the NAFTA. Why? They will because Mexico relies heavily on imports to meet its capital goods requirement and
March 31, 1993

Canadian products are already at the front of the line with Mexican buyers.
As Mexico continues to develop economically and upgrade its facilities opportunities for Ontario machinery and industrial equipment producers will increase. Mr. Bemie Halligan of Novenco Fans Canada Inc. in Cambridge said: "Free trade with Mexico is long overdue". His company makes large industrial fans and a 15 per cent to 20 per cent duty must be paid on their entry into Mexico. The trade deal will in time remove those duties and Mr. Halligan says this will help them a great deal.
Ontario's telecommunications and information technology is another sector that will enjoy expanded opportunities due to the NAFTA. Mexico is striving to modernize its economy and the government is dedicated to developing a more sophisticated telecommunications infrastructure. The Mexican government is also deregulating and privatizing its telecommunications sector. Who but Canada has better knowledge and expertise in telecommunications?
Put these factors together and they add up to fantastic growth in Mexican demand. By the year 2000 it is expected that Mexico will import 42 per cent more telecommunication products and demand for imported information technology will increase by more than 30 per cent in the next five years.
Ontario based companies such as Northern Telecom and Telesat are already active in the Mexican market. Systemhouse, an Ottawa based company, has already signed a $500 million contract with the Mexican government in the anticipation of growth. Yet the members opposite from both parties want to prevent these companies from taking part in that growth market in Mexico.
As well, the NAFTA improves Ontario's ability to attract investment dollars because it gives companies thinking of locating in Ontario the knowledge that they can sell their products to a market of 360 million consumers in North America.
These accomplishments were achieved while ensuring that important exemptions under the FTA will stay in place in the NAFTA. For instance, the auto pact was preserved as well as the supply management system for dairy and poultry products. Both of these exemptions were critical for Ontario.
Government Orders
The NAFTA also safeguards Ontario's fruit and vegetable growers by allowing Canada to take measures against any sudden surges in Mexican imports, which is very important for the farmers in my constituency of Lincoln.
The people of Ontario have more concerns than just the economic benefits that are afforded to them by the NAFTA. That is why it contains more environmental provisions than any other trade agreement and it forbids countries from lowering their environmental standards in order to attract investment.
Just as I must watch out for the implications of the agreement to my riding and province, as Minister of State for Transport I must think how this will affect the portfolio for which I am responsible. For the first time in any international trade agreement transportation modes are included.
In transportation services, the trucking industry has been opened up to allow greater freedom for Canadian shippers to carry cargo to other countries. Under the NAFTA an important issue was the ability to take on cargo in the U.S. for onward transportation to Mexico.
It also allows them to make the return trip, picking up cargo in Mexico and delivering it to the U.S. or Canada. This right will open up over a six-year period but Canadian carriers will maintain the exclusive right of carrying goods from one Canadian point to another Canadian point.
The North American free trade agreement is the most progressive in surface transportation, with provisions for bus, rail and truck modes. It provides detailed schedules for opening up Mexico's closed market for international bus and truck services. The standards regulating safety will be harmonized, also under a detailed schedule, to make sure that Canada's high standard of safety in transportation will be maintained.
As minister, I am keenly aware of the truckers' concerns and I know that Canadian truckers welcome this opening and are anxious to work the U.S. and Mexico border as soon as possible. Toronto is closer to Nuevo Laredo than it is to Edmonton or Vancouver. Imagine how Canadian truckers would feel if the Alber-ta-B.C. market swelled overnight to 85 million consum-

March 31, 1993
Government Orders
ers from 8 million. Eighty per cent of freight shipped across the U.S.-Mexican border is carried in trucks. With the surge of trade between Canada and Mexico the truck traffic will also increase. As Mexico develops and purchases more goods from Canada, Canadian truckers will benefit.
With respect to railway transportation, one of the NAFTA's key advantages is the guarantee of no more restrictions at any level of government. The current degree of openness is locked in. Our major railways have become truly North American in trackage and international in outlook. This has happened in a logical response to shifting market realities, a reality that is confirmed by the NAFTA. I am pleased to see that our railways have recast their operations and are preparing themselves for an integrated North American market.
Transportation in Canada is undergoing historical changes which can only help it face the realities of the North American transportation picture. There is no question that the foundations of a fully integrated North American market with strong Canadian companies taking the lead were laid long before the NAFTA. The NAFTA builds on those foundations and opens up exciting new challenges for the transportation industry and Canadians in general. These are prospects that we should all look forward to.
I am not saying that the NAFTA will revolutionize the economy of Canada. What it will do is open new doors and take the tariffs off some of the old ones. Companies in my home province of Ontario are already looking into the Mexican market so they can hit the ground running once the NAFTA takes effect. In the end, Canada will be stronger.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment and ask a small question.
Approximately 30 years ago the Canadian government signed the Columbia River Treaty with the Americans. At that time we were told how wonderful it was going to be, how it was going to create these great lakes at the back of the dams and so on. Now, 30 years later, we have a situation where in my riding of Kootenay East the Americans are taking this water faster than it can run in. They are opening their dams. They have increased the flow on their dams below from 4,000 cubic feet a second to 22,000 cubic feet a second. Fish and everything are going through the turbines and are being chewed up. Dust bowls are created in the reservoirs behind.
At the time when the Columbia River Treaty was signed we told them that this was going to happen. They are now talking about diverting the Thompson River in Kamloops into the Mica reservoir to create some more water for those greedy Americans who are after our water. It was supposed to be for flood control and hydroelectricity. It is now being used by the Americans for many other uses, such as irrigation, fish enhancement, tourism and other things and we are paying the price with dust bowls and other kinds of things behind the reservoir.
My question is with regard to the water issue. What is to stop the Mexicans or the Americans 10 years from now from saying that it is unfair competition because Canada has all this water and it can create these kinds of fruits and vegetables and these kinds of things? What is to stop them from saying it is unfair to them that they are starving for water?
They have excluded raw logs. Why was that phrase, excluding Canadian waters, not put in there to ensure that there would not be that kind of a debate after we have signed the treaty, 10 years down the road, after everyone has made their changes with regard to their industrial structure and so on?
Then all of a sudden they will say they are going to take our water and I would like to see how we could stop them, because we cannot stop them now under the Columbia River Treaty. I would like to know how we will be able to do it under this treaty.

Mr. Speaker, the Columbia water treaty was a water treaty. This is a trade agreement. In this trade agreement water is not considered as a good for trade. Therefore there is no danger in this trade agreement of opening it up for water. We are trading goods, we are not trading natural resources.
The agreement that the hon. member mentioned is one that was not a trade agreement but a water agreement. I think he is mixing apples and oranges, or perhaps beer and water.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question. While the subcommittee was hearing on transportation issues, Donald Reimer, chief executive officer of Reimer Express Enterprises Limited
March 31, 1993

and chairman of the Sectoral Advisory Group on International Trade for Transportation Services, appeared before the committee. He explained that to complete the competitive picture, efficiencies not only have to be achieved in the production process but also in the transportation links in servicing the customer.
He pointed out that the NAFTA is the first international agreement that attempts to deal with transportation services. He also said that while the agreement also deals with the national treatment of investment and cross-border services, the biggest gain for the transportation industry was increased access to a market that currently totally forbids foreign ownership and operation of transport services.
It should not come as a great surprise that he is supportive of the NAFTA. I would like to ask the minister if she could add to those comments because I am sure they do not come as a great surprise to her.

Mr. Speaker, Mr. Reimer is recognized in this country as being one of the leaders in the transportation industry. We see his trucks from coast to coast, across the border and down into the U.S.
Mr. Reimer is right in saying that this is the first time that we have had transportation included, both from an investment standpoint and a carrying standpoint. It is definitely going to be an advantage as far as Canadian truckers are concerned.
I might also add that it is not only on the carriage of goods but also the investment and working within the transportation industry. In fact, I was reading today that AMF, one of Montreal's largest manufacturing employers, which dismantles and remanufactures locomotives, has recently signed a $5 million contract with Mexico state-owned railway to remanufacture 23 engines with the promise of other components on the horizon.
This is another firm, this time in the province of Quebec, that also sees the opportunity in Mexico for additional business, which means additional jobs in Canada. That is another reason that this deal is good for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-115 that is before us tonight, on the North American free trade agreement, stands before us just after we put into place a few hours ago a time allocation for discussion on this very important next initiative in the free trade agreement.
Government Orders
The question really is: Are we facing a democratic process? Are we allowing the voices of the people to be heard and their concerns considered in the light of this Draconian move to close down the discussions in this House and summarily silence the voices and views that need to be heard with respect to the concerns, and they are many, that we find with regard to the free trade agreement being extended not only to the United States but also south to Mexico.
I would like to recall to members of this House that it was in the dead of winter after a long election campaign in 1988 that we sat late into the night while the government again pushed its agenda through at that time. The question is how many times are we going to have closure and how many times will the government stifle debate when it is determined to get its agenda on the Canada-U.S. agreement approved by Parliament? I do not think that that is the way democracy should work.
We have had closure 25 times. Closure stifles exchange, debate and hearings on major issues of concern that are affecting small, medium and large businesses in this country.
If one looks at the number of times that we have had closure I can say that we have had closure more often than we did since 1913 in this country.
We had this special session that I referred to on the free trade agreement. Little did we think back then that we would be here again today witnessing the same Draconian closure measures on yet another trade deal. It reminds me of that old expression: "The more things change the more they stay the same".
It is that I stand here with the Conservative government opposite shutting down debate, cutting off discussion and abbreviating the democratic process.
With respect to this NAFTA agreement, it is not that Liberals are not open and are not free traders. It is when the deal is right, when it is in the best interests of Canada and when it answers the questions we want to have answered that we support agreements that would enhance trade. I just remind this House that the automotive trade was a very good deal for Canada and it was carefully negotiated in a sectoral agreement and it has been in our best interests. We just heard the minister talking about how wonderful the automotive trade pact has been.

Government Orders
However, that is not the case with the free trade agreement. Unfortunately, this is not in Canada's best interests. It is not just some of the workers who are not going to benefit from this, it is most of the workers in Canada and not just the lucky few.
We said the deal was not needed in 1988 the way it was drafted because it was not the right deal. We said we needed adjustment policies and programs to ease the way into this new global economy. Little did Canadians realize that the trade deal was the government's adjustment program. That is a rather sad comment. It introduced its sink or swim approach to the economy without the benefit of help or assistance for anyone, without helping businesses succeed and most importantly without helping workers prepare for what was ahead. Survival of the fittest it professed. Sink or swim it said. Good luck it said. Canadians have suffered all these years since 1988 as a result.
Yes, there have been some success stories and some winners. However, they are very few and far between and not to the extent that was promised in the high and extravagant words that accompanied this deal with the government. They were not realized by the business community of Canada.
So I say again that we are free traders but on proper terms. The terms of this deal are not right. We say today that the NAFTA deal needs improvement. It needs amendments. It is not complete and it should not be approved in the way it stands.
Mr. Speaker, I draw to your attention that the minister has made some rather extravagant statements. He claims that Canadian exports prove the benefits of the free trade agreement and that the government's economic policies have been right. It is the trickle-down philosophy. I believe he said some things which I think we should examine a little more closely.
Let us take a closer look. The truth is that Canada's trade situation has been steadily declining under the Conservatives and particularly since the free trade agreement came into effect. The minister said that merchandise exports in 1992 reached a high record of $157 billion, 11 per cent higher than in 1991.
What does the evidence show? What is the hard evidence coming from Statistics Canada? It says that our merchandise trade performance is measured by the balance of exports minus imports.
The global merchandise imports for 1992 also reached a record high of $148 billion. As a result, our global trade surplus for 1992 which is $9.5 billion is the smallest in any year dating back to 1981.
So what?

Our trade surplus in 1982, $17.7 billion, was nearly double the figure for 1992.1 hope the Minister of Labour can understand the difference in the figures. That is the "so what". We did much better before than we do today.
Second, the Minister for International Trade said that merchandise exports to the United States in 1992 reached a record high of $122.3 billion. He said that that was 13.6 per cent higher than in 1991.
What are the facts? The facts are that imports from the United States in 1992 also reached a record high of $104.6 billion. Our trade performance with the United States was undeniably better before the free trade agreement and before Tory economic policies came into full effect.
Our cumulative trade surplus for the four years before the free trade agreement was $69.1 billion. It is 14.4 per cent higher than our trade balance for the four years following the free trade agreement which is $60.4 billion.
I would suggest that before such extravagant statements are made, this government should give serious thought to the 1.6 million Canadians who are out of work, which is the highest number among the OECD countries-or perhaps the second highest. Second, it should put into place the kinds of promises about concerns for the work force and concerns for the industries so that they could adapt to what could be a proper trade agreement on a fair and level playing field.
My colleagues from Etobicoke and Winnipeg said that the government should take advantage of the parallel talks that the government is in the middle of right now on environment and on labour standards to press the United States for something that Canada needs badly, which is a definition of trade-distorting subsidies to head off trade disputes with the United States.
March 31, 1993

They recommended to the government that it could just take the GATT wording, insert it into the North American free trade agreement and that should work quite well. It is not such a difficult thing.
The NAFTA has failed to include a subsidies code. It means that we will continue to suffer U.S. trade harassment despite the government's rhetoric now on the two trade deals that were supposed to deliver secure U.S. access.
That certainly takes away from the "free" in these trade deals. It is certainly not the perfect world sold to the voters by the Conservatives or the massive third-party, big-business advertising in 1988.
Now, later, we have learned about these tricks, the trompe-Voeil and the use of your big-business friends. Now when Canadians see a NAFTA campaign coming up they know to look beyond the slick packaging at the real substance.
To improve this trade deal we made it very clear. We have to have an anti-dumping safeguard put into place. This is another serious shortcoming of this agreement. One adds that to the need for a subsidy code.
Another issue raised of significance by the Liberal trade critic for making a proper trade deal was that we would need parallel accords in place on labour standards and on the environment before this House gives approval to this incomplete NAFTA agreement.
Can one imagine buying a house from a home builder who says: "Do not worry, I will finish the roof next week. Just pay me now." I think a lot of us would do far better than that. We would say: "I trust you, perhaps, but I will have a signed dotted line, thank you", or "I will have the completed house before I sign on that line".
That is just not good enough as one can well understand for Canadian people to buy essentially a pig in a poke. We are free traders. I have said that the terms of this agreement leave some pretty large holes on a subsidies code and on labour and environment standards. These make serious shortcomings in this agreement. I would like to briefly turn to the subject of culture and paint a bit of the picture which I have witnessed over the last four or five years in terms of how this Conservative government and the direct and indirect effect of its trade policies and trade deals have affected a precious Canadian resource that is not energy or minerals, although
Government Orders
they are important, but culture which defines us as a people.
I find the NAFTA cultural debate a bit of a dejd vu because once again we hear the government itself asserting that it has protected Canada's cultural sovereignty. This is a country where three out of four books sold originate outside of it, where three out of four dollars earned through the film production industry and the distribution industry end up in foreign owned coffers, where more than three out of four magazines sold on the news stands originate from outside of it and where nine out of ten recordings bought are made from imported master tapes. This is not a culturally sovereign country. I would say that it is a culturally occupied land.
We ought to be speaking and protecting our right to become culturally sovereign to ensure that Canadians retain the tools to develop in that direction. Canadians must gain control of the production and distribution of our cultural products.
A couple of years ago on Momingside Peter Gzowski conducted an informal survey asking for the equivalent of the well-known phrase: "As American as apple pie". The winner was: "As Canadian as possible under the circumstances". The answer may be amusing but it answers somewhat and points out the fragility of Canadian cultural expression and that government policy and programs are crucial to its development.
The problems are structural. Films, books, magazines and sound recordings are the key instruments in letting Canadians gain access to their culture. In the face of technological changes and market advantages of foreign multinational companies our home-grown industries face an increasingly difficult task in gaining access to our Canadian audiences. As a result, Canadians are not able to gamer a fair share of the Canadian market sufficient to reinvest in the production of more Canadian materials.
While Canadians are filling more of their leisure time with cultural activities, the cultural products that they are consuming are from foreign countries.
It is unfortunate but foreign owned multinationals clearly dominate the most lucrative sectors of the Canadian cultural market. Through vertical integration of their corporate structures they often control both production and distribution. In short they have a bloc on the market and in the larger sense they see Canada as the backyard. The only tool that we have that can crack the

Government Orders
lock and allow Canadian artists and consumers access to their own markets is government policy and partnership with business.
Canadian governments at all three levels have created a handful of government policies and programs that have significantly helped Canadian artists and companies to gain access to their own domestic markets.
I am not going to outline all the initiatives. We all understand the importance of Bill C-58, its impact on the magazine industry concerning Sports Illustrated and the whole argument that is going on about that. It underscores the sensitivity that there is to the undertaking through Bill C-58 which has helped us grow as an industry.
If we believe that creators play vitally important roles in our society, that they help us to see ourselves as we really are, warts and all, that they also stand as role models for future generations, then their success and the importance of promoting our young artists and encouraging them to blaze new trails and chase new artistic visions is veiy vital.
It is not that we want to silence other voices. We do not want to close ourselv.es off. We want to be open to the world but we want to have a choice. We have many, many artists crossing the borders and we need that. We want the flow back and forth. We are delighted with our neighbours but we insist on the right to be able to be present and be accountable for and to be perceived in this country. Is that so unreasonable?
What concerns me about this NAFTA text is that with respect to culture it is virtually a repeat of the Canada-U.S. text. The cultural exemption for cultural industries found in the free trade agreement is also in NAFTA. In addition, the definition of cultural industries has been expanded to include persons working in those industries, such as performers and writers.
I say to you, the case in the Canada-U.S. agreement, the cultural exemption, was not complete then and it is not complete now. It held its infamous notwithstanding clause, like a sword of Damocles over our heads then, when each country reserved the right to take measures
of equivalent commercial effect in response to any action regarding cultural industries and that remains.
I want to talk about the dumping below the price it cost of films, videos and sound recordings into this country, but I think that is pretty obvious to all of us.
Five years after the FTA there are still many unanswered questions concerning that notwithstanding clause. For starters, how will commercial effect be measured? Will measures of redress taken by the injured party be directed solely to the cultural industries or possibly to other sectors?
Who will decide what actions are inconsistent and result in negative measures? Does this mean that Canadians will not gain control of their movie screens through much-needed film distribution legislation? What about raising the level of Canadian content on television and radio? What about buy Canadian textbook policies in our schools? Could all future cultural initiatives fall victim? Will our culture become stagnant and not be allowed to grow?
The government points to its success in keeping culture off the trade table, but the true measure of the cultural success of the government can only be in its cultural outputs and Canada is still a culturally occupied country. We incur an annual cultural trade deficit in excess of $1.1 billion to the United States through the importation of films, sound recordings, books and magazines.
There are initiatives that we can take that would be very helpful so that we have Canadian owned and controlled companies. We create our own distribution system separate from the Americans for the dissemination of cultural products and we can see other measures.
You are indicating that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker. I would like to say to you that Liberals are free and fair traders, but I would like to know what this government's hurry is with respect to getting NAFTA done now rather than getting it done right. Is it prudent to push NAFTA through the House before the other signatories? The United States and Mexico, in particular, have signed off on it.
Is it not asking too much that our legislature deal with this agreement before the Clinton administration even
March 31, 1993

submits it to its Congress? It is asking questions about the drug bill that is in there and the constraints of drugs.
Quite simply, this is not a done deal. It is not complete in terms of substance, in terms of process on both of these counts. I agree with my Liberal colleagues who have spoken in the Elouse that the NAFTA legislation should not be approved at the present time and in its present form.
There are some serious worries in here and I would really like to ask the government to put this aside for the moment. Let us see what the Americans are going to bring in, what the Mexicans say.
On behalf of all my constituents I can promise them not only north-south trade, but east and west trade. It will be the best kind of trade with a well prepared work force, a well prepared industry, so that we can truly move forward in the interests of our people and certainly give some hope to the youth and the 1.6 million who are out there unemployed today.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the principle of trilateral free trade. However, something is bothering me in this whole matter. Why is government in such a hurry to sign this free trade deal, NAFTA, when we know that the American President Bill Clinton has requested a little more time to negotiate with Mexico in particular on the issues of labour standards and the environment? Why is this government in such a rush to ratify this agreement? It would put the US government in an awkward position if one of its partners had already ratified the agreement, as it were. I think that the US government would be in an uncomfortable position to negotiate with Mexico if we were to pass this bill as is without having had the opportunity, as Canadians, to negotiate the environmental and human rights issues. I say it would be rather embarrassing for the Americans.
To have a North American economic pact, I am all for it. But let us give the Americans the chance to negotiate or to bring pressure to bear on Mexico in the future regarding the environment and human rights.
We cannot interfere in Mexican government business. They can settle their own disputes. However, we can now
Government Orders
pressure Mexico into gradually doing better in terms of environment and human rights.
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the hon. member for Mount Royal why she does not come out and say straight out that she is for free trade, but that her support is conditional on the respect of human rights and the environment in Mexico. Why say that she is for global trade liberalization? Why not say straight out that she is against trilateral free trade, against having a strong North American deal allowing us to compete with the European Community and the ASEAN for instance? I think we need such a North American economic pact to compete with other economic pacts, I put the question to the hon. member for Mount Royal.

I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but maybe the hon. member for Longueil arrived late while I was making my speech. What I said was that the Liberals have always been in favour of free trade, a free trade with equal treatment and fair play, and that we wanted arrangements to be made with Americans and Mexicans on the environment and labour standards and also on other issues that had to be settled before we could promote and pass this bill here in the House. Mr. Speaker, I totally agree that the Liberals have always been free traders. But I would really like you to be aware, if you are not already-and I will say it in my mother tongue of our global trade performance with respect to the way the Conservatives have managed our economy.

For the year 1992 we show a merchandise trade deficit with every one of our principal trading areas other than the United States. Our cumulative trade surplus in the four years before the free trade agreement came into effect was $47.9 billion and fell 26.9 per cent-that is 27 per cent-in the years following the free trade agreement to $35 billion.

The hon. member is absolutely right. We forgot our eastern and western trade partners, and we concentrated on programs that were harmful to Canada because we did not put in place the programs required to face global changes and to make our workers and our industries competitive.

I thank the hon. member who agrees with me. In its present form, the bill is not good. We must fix certain things before we can proceed.

Mr. Speaker, I know others are looking to take the floor and I will not be very long.
First I would like to congratulate my colleague, the member for Mount Royal on her speech. I agree with a fair amount of what she had to say. A fair amount in Restigouche-Chaleur is about 99.9 per cent.
When I look at the NAFTA and when people out there look at the NAFTA they wonder if it can be simplified somewhat. Who can really say what is wrong and what is right with it.
The problem with the NAFTA is that there is no definition of a subsidy, no definition of dumping, it lacks environmental standards and proper labour standards. That puts it in its simplest form so that everyone can understand what is wrong with NAFTA. To me that is what is wrong with it.
I would like to ask the hon. member if she could maybe explain a little more of that aspect, whether she agrees with that comment or not and maybe to go on a little more.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that we are 99.4 per cent in agreement.
No, I did not say that.

I guess I did not speak clearly enough or else I have not expressed myself in the most succinct way. You said in the shortest and most succinct fashion exactly what it took me 20 minutes to say in my speech. I agree with everything you have said so I guess we are 100 per cent in accord.

Mr. Speaker, it has been very interesting to listen to the debate on the NAFTA today. For better or for worse, we certainly know where the Conservatives stand. It becomes much more complicated when one listens to the Liberals. Some love it, some hate it, but it does seem at base, most love it more than they hate and would like it mostly to remain the same.
Let there be no mistake, there is only one party and one party only in this country whose opposition to the
North American free trade agreement is unequivocal and that is the New Democratic Party. NAFTA is a bad deal for Canadians. It is impossible to renegotiate. No parallel accord can fix it. It must not proceed.
We are on record and I think have shown in our international affairs as well as nationally that this party is a great believer in fair trade. NAFTA is not fair trade and believe me NAFTA is not free for Canada. Anyone who believes that has been sold a bill of goods.
Let us look at the agreement logically. If NAFTA were simply a free trade agreement, the text of the agreement would consist of one line and one line only. There will be no tariffs between Canada, the United States and Mexico. Instead it is not one line, it is thousands of pages. It is not just a simple commercial agreement about tariffs. It is an economic constitution and it is changing the economic constitution of Canada and of North America. It is a constitution that diminishes the rights of Canadians, that exports our jobs, that sells off our resources at bargain prices and weakens the ability of our governments to do what they are elected to do, serve the people.
Canadians deserve a clear voice that says: "We do not accept these unfair trade arrangements and we believe they must be stopped".

What in NAFTA is really destructive for Canada? Since I have only 10 minutes I will keep the list short.
First, the changes in the rules of origin as they apply to textiles are going to play havoc in the clothing industry where tens of thousands of jobs are going to disappear.
Secondly, there is no Canadian content rule for cars, only North American, not Canadian. The Auto Pact does not mean anything anymore and jobs will move south.
Third, NAFTA is going even further than the free trade agreement in the elimination of price and export controls on our energy resources.
Fourth, there is a real danger that our water might be exported in great quantities. Water is not excluded from the agreement.
Fifth, NAFTA prevents the Canadian government, in the case of foreign take-over, from negotiating conditions such as, technology transfers and keeping Canadians as executives.
March 31, 1993



Sixth, NAFTA accelerates the destructive policy of deregulation that we have seen in the air industry but particularly in cross-border trucking and in telecommunications.
Seventh, NAFTA enshrines forever this government's bill that sold out to the multinational drug companies. The drug companies are in for a windfall while prices for consumers go up and we are told to cut back on health care.
Eighth, under NAFTA a Crown corporation set up by a province or federally to promote non-commercial objectives such as energy conservation or an airline service to remote communities could be forbidden. NAFTA restricts the government's ability to ensure secondary processing of our resources, an absolutely essential prerequisite to developing our regional economies and moving into the 21st century.
Ninth, the NAFTA restricts government's capacity to promote regional development.
Let us be clear what we are talking about. We are talking about a deal that takes the power out of the hands of people and their democratically elected institution and puts it into the hands of multinational corporations that are unelected and unaccountable to the Canadian people.
I say with regret that the government in power, the Conservative Party, did everything it could do to destroy government and to diminish the democracy in this country. This time it will not get away with it.
I briefly mentioned some of the objectionable elements in the NAFTA but equally dangerous is what is not there. There is nothing to prevent continued U.S. trade harassment. U.S. trade law will continue to prevail. There is no definition of subsidies or process to define them. There are no minimum labour standards. There are no minimum environmental standards. There is no addressing of human rights issues.

There is nothing in the agreement to keep firms leaving Canada from exploiting Mexican workers who work for starvation wages under horrendous conditions and in a life threatening environment.
Government Orders
The time has come to make it perfectly clear that people have not been put on this earth to serve commercial interests but rather that trade must serve the interests of the people.

We have to ask the question why the Conservative government is so intent on ramming through this legislation. It is not finished in the United States. Questions are being raised in caucus. Some of the signators have raised many questions-human rights in Mexico, rights for workers, the environment-and yet this government pursues and says in Canada we want to get this legislation through right now.
There can be only one answer: an outgoing Prime Minister wants a monument; an outgoing trade minister wants a monument. Mr. Speaker, we will build them a statue. It will be cheaper.
Hear, hear.

It is absolutely ludicrous to proceed with this legislation when NAFTA is not even complete. There are discussions going on about parallel accords, some of which would fundamentally affect the NAFTA as it is now and yet the Canadian government is saying it is going to pass it in Canada. We are brave in Canada. We will not even wait until it is finished to pass it. We just rush right in and pass it. We do not even wait to see the finished product. That is bad business. It is bad democracy.
I would ask what kind of bargaining power it gives us with our partners in the NAFTA. We go to the table. They are negotiating perhaps parallel agreements or other changes to the NAFTA and we say it is okay because we have already passed it in Canada, but we would really like to negotiate this. It does not make any sense. It is ludicrous, not even logical. It is certainly bad bargaining. It is definitely bad logic.
Finally, I want to raise a question that is puzzling to me. Why does this government not want to allow a full debate on this issue?
I find it interesting that last week as this government was shutting down debate on the NAFTA legislation a candidate for the Tory leadership talked about the politics of inclusiveness. I guess that candidate felt that six hours of debate on the second reading of a bill is adequate. I should explain for those who are watching that second reading is the principle of the bill. It is

March 31, 1993
Government Orders
extremely important because people have a chance during that debate to talk not just about what is in the bill but the very foundation on which that bill is built, the
very ideology.
We know that the trade deal is there to entrench Tory policies. The Liberals agree so it entrenches theirs too and it is easier for them to have a Conservative government than to do it themselves. We understand that.
There really can be no reason for ramming through a bill which is so fundamental to the future of Canada. To talk about the politics of inclusiveness is a joke. As I said, we will have had about six hours of debate on this bill. We have had longer debates on bills that certainly were important, but not as fundamental to the future of this country and of our children and grandchildren than this bill. Yet the government says six hours. That is it; it is closing it down.
If these are the the politics of inclusiveness from a member of this government that has invoked closure and used time allocation to shut down debate more than any government in the history of Canada, it will not work and Canadians will not let the government get away with it.
This bill deserves a real debate. Canadians deserve the opportunity to see a full debate, to participate in a full debate, to have all the information and to know that their representatives have had the opportunity to express their views and had the opportunity to explore the alternatives, to explore on what the bill is based as well as the contents of the bill. It is not good enough to stop the voices and views of Canadians. There is no rush and we on this side of the House say, Prime Minister, step in, give democracy a chance.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to just take the final five minutes left to me to put this on the record. The member from Winnipeg had talked about one of the impacts of the NAFTA.
The Western Canadian Wheat Growers which represents some 7,000 farmers made a presentation before the subcommittee. It was interesting to learn that exports of agricultural commodities account for 50 per cent of their farm revenue. In the grains and oilseeds example they said that in 1991 they exported 62,000 tonnes to Mexico. It was only 62,000 tonnes because of restrictive import licensing requirements. But in 1991-92 the requirements were eased somewhat by the Mexican government. For crop year 1991-92 exports went up to 492,000 tonnes. What will happen under NAFTA is that the licensing requirements will be eliminated entirely and immediately-
Members may wonder what the duty rate is now on wheat going to Mexico. Currently, the maximum duty is 50 per cent. What will happen after the signing of NAFTA is that tariff rate will be reduced to 15 per cent immediately and will be phased out over 10 years. I was surprised that the Liberal member from western Canada would not be supportive of NAFTA when indeed it is

most beneficial for wheat farmers, as they indicated when the subcommittee was in Winnipeg.
I have a few other points I would like to put on the record. People should understand how important exports are to Canada, because Canada does not have a large population. The population of Canada is currently 27 million. Everyone talks about exports coming in from Japan, but everyone forgets that Japan has a large domestic economy. Therefore, in actual fact about 13.5 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product is exported from Japan because of its large domestic market. The United States with a population of 250 million obviously has a lot of consumers. Therefore only about 10 per cent of its GNP is as a result of exports. But in Canada, with only 27 million people, Canadian manufacturers produce more than we can consume. Therefore almost 30 per cent of Canada's Gross Domestic Product has to be exported.
The issue becomes on value added. Everyone says that the only things Canadians can export are the raw resources so why trade with the United States, why do we not trade with other countries, why do we not trade with Japan?
The facts are that of our trade with Japan, 5 per cent of it are finished goods and 95 per cent of it are semi-finished goods and raw materials. Japan is not a big consumer of value added products. About 25 per cent of our exports to the European Community are value added products and 75 per cent of it are semi-finished or raw materials, but to the United States a large amount of our exports indeed are value added.
My time is short and I wish I had the opportunity to give all the statistics. The C.D. I wanted to address the issue this raises concerning our treatment of waste.
The green plan identified waste as one of the most serious problems facing industrialized countries like Canada, particularly, that have the luxury of being able to waste.

speechtext:

However the solution to Canada's environmental problems will not be solved by blue boxes alone. Canada produces over 30 million tonnes of garbage annually. That is more than a tonne of garbage for every man, woman and child in Canada.
We recycle only 10 per cent of our garbage and send most of the remainder to rapidly filling land sites. In Canada collection and disposal costs of waste exceed $1.5 billion annually.
The green plan gives a great deal of attention to the treatment of waste and to how we can reduce waste. It says that Canada's goal is to cut waste by 50 per cent by the year 2000. Managing waste inefficiently imposes an economic burden on Canadians. It goes on to say that Canadians are well aware of their poor waste manage-

March 31, 1993

ment practices. They recognize that one of the more important challenges we face in moving this country toward sustainable development is reducing the volumes of waste we produce.
In October 1989 the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment adopted as its goal the reduction of waste in Canada by 50 per cent by the year 2000.
We are getting very close to halfway toward 2000 since that target was set by all the environment ministers of our nation and we have not in fact made a great deal of progress.
This motion before the House asks us to take a strong position on a major component of the waste stream, and that is paper. Paper products account for 1.4 million tonnes of Ontario's annual residential waste. That was in 1989 so we can be sure it is significantly higher now. Newsprint, fine paper and magazines alone account for close to one million tonnes.
We are worried about our forests. We are worried about forests at home. We are worried about forests around the world. If we recycled 50 per cent of our waste paper then almost 50 million trees would be saved each year.
This motion addresses an important portion of the paper waste that goes into our dumps every year. It is an important portion of the tens of millions of trees that are needlessly cut and wasted every year. This motion addresses itself specifically to unaddressed advertising mail. Many people across this country call it junk mail because they do not want it in their mailboxes, they do not want to be left with the problem of disposing of it, they are tired of receiving material that they do not want in the first place and even with the greatest conscientiousness they cannot even recycle it. There were 14 billion pieces of unaddressed advertising that were distributed in Canada last year. That is 560 pieces-close to two a day-for every man, woman and child in Canada. That means several thousand pieces of unwanted unsolicited mail coming into Canadians' homes every day.
Not all of that is delivered by Canada Post Corporation. However, Canada Post Corporation is delivering 25 per cent of it and is the largest single deliverer of junk mail to Canadian homes.
Private Members' Business
We are not talking here about addressed ad mail or appeals from charities for contributions. That is not what this motion talks about. However, of the 14 billion pieces of junk mail delivered every year in Canada, 25 per cent or 3.5 billion pieces are delivered by Canada Post. Unaddressed junk mail counts for 36 per cent of all the mail pieces that Canada Post delivers but only 6 per cent of its mail delivery revenues.
The volume is going up by 500 million pieces every year. It has gone up from 23 per cent of Canada Post's mail deliveries barely four years ago to 36 per cent in the last full year of reporting. That is an increase that is very dramatic. Remember that every time Canada Post delivers one of these flyers to your home-and it delivers an average of 140 pieces a year for every person in your household-it means that trees have been needlessly cut down.
There was a previous motion in the House to deal with the issue of whether there should be a requirement for advertising mail to be both on recycled and recyclable paper. Regrettably, that was not a votable motion.
There is another aspect to this which perhaps is not directly related to the environmental concerns that prompted me to bring it forward. Clearly the growing intrusion of Canada Post into the delivery of advertising mail is becoming a serious problem for many smaller dailies and weeklies across this country which were receiving a substantial portion of their advertising revenue from delivering advertising mail.
Canada Post getting into this at such a massive rate has had an impact on them. It is taking away from private newspapers across this country, whether weeklies or dailies, and is seriously inhibiting the ability of many small dailies and weeklies to survive, to bring the news to their communities in a way that is responsive to local community information, local community events, as well as giving a local interpretation of regional, national or international events.
A second question I think we should be asking ourselves in this House is why is Canada Post still a public corporation, however temporarily, competing with private sector distributors in their own business area? One of the claims Canada Post made is: "We deliver your mail to your mailbox". Why is it going out and hiring

March 31, 1993
Private Members' Business
people other than the usual postal workers to deliver mail?
I am sure other members of Parliament have had the same complaints as I have had in my office about people walking across their lawn on a Sunday afternoon and dropping material in their mailbox, usually junk mail. They are astounded to find out that this is somebody who has actually been employed by Canada Post to deliver advertising mail to their home.
I want to quote a bit from the report on the first two years on the green plan that was issued just a few days ago by the Minister of the Environment. It states: "The office of waste management will continue to develop communications products to support the promotion of the four rs and the waste campaign under the umbrella of environmental citizenship. A primer on waste management and fact sheets will be produced. The office will work toward developing partnerships to promote the concept of environmental citizenship".
I think we all know that the green plan depends very heavily not only on government and private sector action to achieve its goals, but also on the involvement of citizens. It puts great emphasis on Canadians in all walks of life taking environmental responsibility in their daily activities.
This motion addresses precisely that desire of Canadians to be responsible for their environment. In growing numbers they are saying: "I don't want this material in my mailbox. I don't want the public corporation called Canada Post delivering advertising to me. I want to have the choice". The government talks about environmental choice programs and consumers are saying: "I want to have the choice. I want to be able to say do not drop this on my private property".
When I wrote the minister responsible for Canada Post well over a year ago, it was to ask that he consider amending the legislation to give Canadians that choice, to give them the right to put a sign on the mailbox that they provide for Canada Post's convenience saying: "I do not want any unaddressed advertising mail left at my home".
The minister did not reply but referred it to Canada Post. Of course, Canada Post said that the legislation obliges it to deliver every piece of mail that is consigned
to it by its customers. Of course it does. That is why I had written to the minister asking him to consider changes to the legislation to allow households or businesses to refuse delivery of bulk mail, unaddressed advertising mail by affixing a notice to the mail receptacle. The minister still has yet to reply to that request.
We adopted a national waste reduction plan several years ago. We have made minimal progress on achieving the objectives of that plan. We continue to cut trees unnecessarily because we refuse to use the legislative authority we have in this House to pass the kinds of laws that allow Canadians to exercise their commitment to good environmental citizenship.
If we as parliamentarians are not prepared to give Canadians the tools to act responsibly toward the environment, then I am not sure why we should continue with programs to encourage environmental citizenship. Far too often we do with one hand something to encourage a certain kind of behaviour or to discourage damaging behaviour with respect to the environment. Then with the other hand we undo all that effort by refusing to co-operate with our citizens in exercising that citizenship, in exercising the awareness that we have attempted to create for them.
This is not a revolutionary motion. It is not going to greatly disrupt Canada Post. I know some would say that 6 per cent of Canada Post's revenue is significant. What is more significant is whether this is generating revenue for Canada Post, generating profits, or whether in fact it is being subsidized by the first-class mail rates which we know have increased significantly in the last couple of years. Certainly some of the small community newspapers in this country would claim that Canada Post is competing unfairly by cross-subsidization within its other services.
The motion is to allow us to at least have a committee look at the various ways in which we could assist Canadians to do what they want to do. That is to be better environmental citizens and to control the amount of paper coming to them and to influence the market through their consumerism.
We talk about economic instruments. Consumerism, the power of the consumer, is one of the greatest of those economic instruments. However, if we continue with legislation that does not allow consumers to exercise those choices and therefore to influence business in a positive way to the benefit of the environment, then we
March 31, 1993

can hardly blame Canadians if the amount of garbage generated, if the amount of trees cut down every year continues to increase while our environment continues to deteriorate.
I ask for the favourable consideration of the House of this motion. I seek the unanimous consent of the House to have the subject matter of the motion referred to a committee of the House.
