subsubtopic: ADVERTISING MAIL AND FLYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity today to speak on a matter which is becoming very important for all Canadians.
We are becoming more and more aware of the environmental problems around us. We are more concerned about the state of our environment and what the future holds for us. Canadians are trying harder to improve the situation. Individuals, businesses and all levels of government have recognized their greater responsibility towards the environment. Canada Post acknowledges its responsibility and acts accordingly.
I would like to talk about initiatives Canada Post undertook to play a more active role in the protection of our environment. The corporation realized that the protection and conservation of the environment are crucial to the welfare of its employees, its clients and the communities it serves. That is why it came up with an environmental policy in 1990.
Needless to say, it was not easy for such a big business to implement that kind of program throughout the country. It represented an enormous task which could not be carried out overnight. Canada Post was able to instil more respect for the environment in its everyday operations. For example, paper consumption in its administrative services has been reduced by almost 30 per cent. Publications intended for its employees are printed on recycled paper, using vegetable inks, and its energy and fuel consumption has also been reduced.
Those are only a few of the initiatves taken by the corporation and they show how conscious it is of its responsibility toward the environment.
Private Members' Business
The media are warning us more and more often of the dangers threatening our environment because of our thoughtlessness, and that is starting to work. It is at our own risk that we ignore them.
The responsibility toward environment does not fall to only one person or one organization. All those who contribute to the problem must do their share to find a solution. Looking for a culprit among all those responsible will not help us deal with this crisis.
Just think of the convenience stores for example. They sell products intended for consumers in a hurry. They carry packaged products such as potato chips, chocolate bars and so on. We do not blame this type of retailer for offering too many packaged products; they are only selling them. The solution rests first with those who design the packaging.
The same can be said about a product Canada Post is offering to consumers. We sometimes blame it for distributing this kind of mail, referred to as junk mail by many. For Canada Post, it is Mediapost.
For its customers, Mediapost is an accurate and cost-effective means of transmitting their message. People like David Love, vice-president of the World Wide Nature Fund, stated that: "For charities, mail advertising is not junk mail but the most efficient, personal, ethically acceptable and important of all fund-raising methods."
Mediapost is an important part of postal activities with an annual volume of over 4.7 billion items and some $500 million in annual revenues. It is also an efficent and viable way to deliver a message whether it be from a small comer store owner or a national retailer or charitable organization like the World Wide Nature Fund.
Mediapost is useful, and studies also show that people like to receive direct mail advertising. Mediapost has interesting features. Let me list a few. It can be printed on paper that can be or has been recycled thanks to vegetable based ink. Mediapost is included with your mail so that the wind cannot blow it away. It is delivered directly in the mail box. It is also possible to target a specific group or area. In that way, it can be delivered only to those who should receive it, thus minimizing waste.

March 31, 1993
Private Members' Business
Direct-mail advertising is a big business in Canada. It is an effective and profitable means of communication which provides great benefits to the Canadian economy.
Judge for yourself, Mr. Speaker. Every year, direct mail generates $7.86 billion in sales in Canada. Canadian consumers spend $170 a year on average for goods and services advertised by direct mail. Direct mail accounts for $1.9 billion or 22 per cent of net advertising revenue. It employs over 200,000 Canadians. It is an industry that is growing at a rate of 8 to 10 per cent a year.
Direct mail is an attractive form of interactive communication with many commercial spin-offs. We have nothing to gain and much to lose by eliminating it. What we must all try to do is to find a balance between this economic reality and our environmental responsibility.
Canada Post is a distributor and only one link in a long chain, which begins with an advertiser, someone with a message to send. It could be a retailer, a politician or an organization seeking funds.
The chain continues with an advertising agency that designs the message, and a printer who reproduces it on paper made by a company that processes forest products. Then a direct mail house prepares the message for distribution. Finally, Canada Post, which is near the end of the chain, distributes the message.
Quite a few steps are involved before we can even start distributing an advertising flyer. After delivery it reaches the last link in the chain, the consumer who eventually recycles the flyer, or at least we hope so.
Canada Post is mindful of environmental issues. It has responded to the concerns raised by this kind of advertising in a way that takes into account both environmental and economic factors, but it cannot act alone. It needs the help of all concerned. To find practical solutions, Canada Post must work in co-operation with all advertisers.
That is why the corporation is trying to bring together all industries that have a stake in these issues.
It has set up a committee consisting of announcers, advertising agencies, paper producers, printers, publishers, direct mail advertising companies, distributors, recycling companies and municipal representatives. Together they are trying to develop responsible ways to use paper in advertising. By working together with the other players in this sector, they hope to get products and services that are environmentally friendly.
It is the kind of integrated and systematic approach we need to deal with that all important question facing us today: How do we protect and preserve the environment? If we are to meet the challenges of the future, we must take this comprehensive approach as solutions emerge. We know they will not be lasting solutions unless all parties are prepared to co-operate.
In conclusion, I want to say that I am totally opposed to this bill in its present form.
More and more businesses and industries are trying to find solutions to environmental problems by promoting civic-minded actions. The Canada Post Corporation is no exception. It is a leader among businesses committed to playing an active role in environmental protection.
Canada Post has implemented an environmental policy. It uses recyclable products and it is also engaged in recycling activities. It has reduced its energy consumption as well as the volume of paper used by its employees. The corporation has also limited its fuel consumption.
Those are only a few of the initiatives which demonstrate how serious Canada Post is about the environment.
I conclude by saying that environmental responsibility is up to everyone, including producers, suppliers, distributors and even consumers.
The involvement of individuals, business and all levels of government is crucial. In many instances, solutions to environmental problems are found in a co-operative approach committing all parties to maintaining the delicate balance which exists between environmental and economic factors.
A co-operative approach to the challenges ahead of us will mean that whatever effort we make today to protect our environment will help build a stronger foundation for the environment of tomorrow.
March 31, 1993
